Project 07 · Electron optics

The Electron Beam, from Tip to Measurement

Numa Koudsie · lecture notes and simulations · every number computed

Question. Why does anyone build an electron beam, and what must the machine deliver? Chips have features a few nanometres wide and one defect can kill a chip, so every step is inspected and measured. Light cannot resolve such features; the electron wavelength at kilovolt energies is picometres. The beam is a probe scanned over the wafer, and what comes back gives edge position, height and material. The machine must give a spot thinner than the feature, enough current for a clean picture, a beam gentle enough for fragile resist, and speed, and these demands trade against each other. The chapters expose those trade-offs one by one.

Reading guide for the reviewer

What this page shows
One electron’s way from a sharp metal tip to a measured line width on a wafer, in ten short chapters. The tip emits it (chapter 2), fields accelerate and focus it (chapters 1, 3, 4), the optics squeeze it into a probe a few nanometres wide (chapter 5), it scatters inside the wafer and sends back the signal (chapter 6), and a width is read from that signal with a known precision (chapter 7). Chapter 8 joins the stages into one machine; chapter 9 gathers the threads. Each chapter starts from an everyday picture, derives its formulas, and ends with a simulation whose sliders are the symbols of the formulas. Chapters 0 and 9 can be read alone; the rest build on each other.
What it models
Newton’s and Lorentz’s laws for a charge in fields, with relativity where it matters; field emission by tunnelling; brightness and its conservation; a magnetic lens with Glaser’s bell-shaped field, traced ray by ray; the four blurs of a probe and the best beam angle; the scattering of electrons in silicon, aluminium, copper and gold by a Monte Carlo simulation; the shot noise of counting and the precision of an edge; and the chain of all these, with a sensitivity table and a tolerance study.
What it leaves out
Real pole-piece fields (the lens field is an analytic model, and there is no field solver), aberration correctors, misalignment and coma, the interaction of beam electrons with each other, charging of insulators, resist damage, three-dimensional scattering in a real line, and any detail of a commercial instrument. Where a model is used outside its range (low voltage on heavy elements, for example), the chapter says so and shows the gap to measurements. Spreads and specifications in chapter 8 are stated assumptions.
Where each number comes from
SI units throughout; constants from CODATA 2018. Every number in the text is computed by the project’s code, not typed: every browser module, except the one of chapter eight, which only chains the others, has an independent Python twin that must agree with it, the derivations are checked symbolically, and published data (stopping powers, backscattering measurements, secondary-electron yields, lens coefficients) are shown beside the model with their source. Each chapter ends with its table of checks. Every chapter was also read by two independent reviewers, and what they found is recorded in the project’s audit notes.

10 of 10 chapters written · 100 numbered equations · 13 figures · 776 computed numbers · 8 simulations running in the page. Chapters that are not written yet show as “in preparation”.

Chapter 0The goal

0.1The question

A chip is a few square centimetres of silicon carrying billions of switches. One switch that is the wrong size, or one wire that is cut, can make the whole chip useless, so every manufacturing step is followed by a measurement, and the measuring machine has to look at structures that are only a few nanometres across.

Take the tightest wires of a processor of 2025. The International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS 2022, More Moore, Table MM-7) lists their pitch, the distance from the middle of one wire to the middle of the next, as 20 nm: a line about 10 nm wide, then a gap of the same width, and so on. A hydrogen atom is about a tenth of a nanometre across. The cubic cell of the silicon crystal is 0.543 nm wide (CODATA 2018) and neighbouring atoms are 0.235 nm apart, so a line 10 nm wide is about 43 atoms across. The task is to say, for a line like that, where its edges are, how tall it is and what it is made of, and to say it for millions of lines on a wafer and within minutes, so that a factory can correct its machines before the next wafer is spoiled.

Think of reading a coin in the dark by running a fingertip over it. A finger tells you the coin is round and has a head on it, but the fine engraving is lost, because the fingertip is wider than the lines. A sharp needle can follow them. An electron beam is that needle: a very thin probe that is scanned across the wafer, one point after another, while a detector counts what comes back from each point. This project builds, chapter by chapter, the physics of that needle and of the machine that holds it, and checks each part against theory and published measurements.

0.2Why light is not enough

The obvious probe is light, and light is used for many steps of chip making. It has a limit, and we derive it, because the limit is the reason for the whole project.

Imagine a pattern of lines with period (pitch) p, lit by a plane light wave of wavelength λ in a medium of refractive index n. The pattern acts as a diffraction grating: the light leaves in directions θm​ given by the grating equation p(sinθm​−sinθi​)=mλ/n, where θi​ is the angle of incidence and m=0,±1,±2,… counts the diffraction orders. The picture of the grating is carried by the interference of the orders. If a lens collects only the zeroth order, it sees a uniform bright field and no lines at all. To see lines, at least one more order must enter the lens. A lens can accept rays up to an angle α from its axis; the number NA=nsinα is its numerical aperture. Tilt the illumination to the edge of the aperture, θi​=α, so that the zeroth order enters at +α; the order m=−1 then leaves at sinθ−1​=sinα−λ/(np), and it still enters the lens when this is at least −sinα. That requires λ/(np)≤2sinα:

pmin​=2NAλ​.
(0.1)

This is Abbe's limit (E. Abbe, Arch. mikrosk. Anat. 9, 413, 1873). It is a statement about the period; the smallest line is half of it. Light is therefore limited by two numbers it cannot change much: its wavelength, and the numerical aperture, which cannot exceed the refractive index of the medium. For deep-ultraviolet light of wavelength 193 nm through water (a numerical aperture of 1.35 is a typical value of an immersion tool, and the ceiling is the index of water) pmin​= 71.5 nm, 3.6 times the pitch of 20 nm that we want to look at. With extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light of 13.5 nm, the roadmap's workhorse aperture of 0.33 gives pmin​= 20.5 nm and its high-NA successor of 0.55 gives 12.3 nm. The IRDS lithography chapter says that a half-pitch of 12 nm is "optically resolvable by 0.33 NA optics" (a half-pitch of 10.2 nm by (0.1), so the statement is consistent with the limit), but resists limit it in practice. EUV light is made in a hot tin plasma, is absorbed by every material, even air, and has to be reflected from mirrors in vacuum. It prints patterns; it is not a practical way to look at millions of them quickly on every wafer. Optical measurement of finished patterns works on test targets of many lines and infers a shape from what the whole target does to the light; Applied Materials describes this as "optical target-based approximation, statistical sampling, and single-layer control" and says that leading-edge designs need a metrology that goes beyond it.

0.3Why electrons

An electron is also a wave. Its wavelength is λ=h/p, where h=6.62607015×10−34 Js is Planck's constant and p the momentum (in this paragraph only; elsewhere in the chapter p is the pitch). An electron that has fallen through a voltage V has the kinetic energy T=eV; the relativistic relation between energy and momentum, (pc)2=T(T+2mc2), gives, as chapter 1 derives in §1.5,

λ=2meV(1+2mc2eV​)​h​.
(0.2)

At V=1 kV this is λ= 38.8 pm and at 30 kV it is 6.98 pm (1 pm is a thousandth of a nanometre). The wavelength is 0.071 of the silicon lattice constant at 1 kV and 2866 times smaller than the 20 nm pitch at 30 kV. This settles one thing: the wavelength itself lies far below the features. It does not make diffraction irrelevant. A lens that forms a probe works with beam half-angles α of a few milliradians, and diffraction then blurs the spot by about λ/α, which at 1 kV is a few nanometres, comparable with the lines; chapter 5 balances this blur against the lens aberrations. Figure 0.1 puts the three lengths on one axis.

An electron microscope does not reach a spot of the size of its wavelength, because the lenses that focus electrons are much worse than glass lenses, as chapters 4 and 5 show. The spot is set by the source size, the aberrations of the lenses and the diffraction at the aperture, and this chain is the subject of the project. What the short wavelength buys is that it is not the first limit, so that a better source and better lenses can still improve the picture.

There are three further reasons, each worked out in a later chapter. An electron has the charge −e, so electric and magnetic fields can steer and focus it: chapter 1 describes how, and every lens of chapter 4 is such a field. An X-ray photon has no charge, so no field can steer it; its optics are limited to weak, specialised elements such as zone plates and grazing-incidence mirrors, though its wavelength is short. An ion has the charge and a short wavelength as well, but it is thousands of times heavier (a proton alone is 1836 times the electron mass), and at kilovolt energies it knocks atoms out of the surface it is meant to examine; an electron of the same energy mostly does not (chapter 6). And what comes back is useful: electrons of the surface layer, which carry the shape, and backscattered electrons from deeper layers, which carry the material (chapter 6).

0.4What the machine has to deliver

The probe has to do four things at once, and they pull against each other.

The spot must be thinner than the structure, or every measurement averages over neighbours. The current in the spot must be large enough that the picture is clean: electrons arrive one at a time, so the number counted in a pixel fluctuates by the square root of the number (shot noise), and a clean edge needs thousands of counts. The beam must be gentle enough for fragile resist, which a fast electron damages, and still reach buried layers, which a slow electron cannot, so the landing energy is a compromise. And it must be fast, because a factory measures many wafers an hour. A smaller spot means less current, because the electrons come from a source of finite brightness; less current means longer dwell time per pixel, and so slower measurement. Chapters 2 to 8 follow these dependences quantitatively.

The state of the art can be read off the public statements of one manufacturer. Applied Materials says on the product page of its PROVision 10 system (read on 9 November 2026) that the column uses "cold field emission (CFE) technology", that it reaches "up to 100 million accurate, actionable measurements per hour", that its Elluminator "captures 95% of back-scattered electrons", and that it offers "high-energy modes for rapid measurement, hundreds of nanometers deep, and low-energy modes for damage-free measurement of fragile materials and structures, including EUV and high-NA EUV photoresist". In the press release of 14 December 2022 it contrasts "thermal field emission" sources, operated at "more than 1,500°C", with cold field emission, "a narrower beam with more electrons", "sub-nanometer image resolution and a 10X increase in imaging speed". The price is a vacuum "well below" 10−11 millibar (the release prints "1×10 – 11"), two to three orders of magnitude better than for thermal sources, because "if a single atom adheres to the eBeam source tip, it can partially block the emission of electrons", and a "cyclical self-cleaning process". We quote these as public claims by the manufacturer. This project is not affiliated with Applied Materials, does not use its data, and models no product of the company; it builds the physics from the first principles that every such column rests on, and the statements above show which behaviour those principles must be able to explain: why a cold tip is bright but fragile, why a vacuum of 10−9 pascal matters, why a high-energy mode sees deeper.

Chapter 1A free electron in fields

1.1A beam you can bend

Switch on an old cathode-ray television in a dark room and bring a bar magnet close to the glass. The picture twists, colours smear, and when you take the magnet away it settles back. Nothing touched the screen. The magnet reached through the glass and pushed on something invisible inside, and the push changed with the direction the something was moving.

That something is a beam of electrons. In 1897 J. J. Thomson built a tube like the one drawn in Figure 1.1, pumped it until almost nothing was left inside, and did with a battery and two coils what the magnet does to the television. His goal was to find out what the beam was made of. The same two handles, an electric field and a magnetic field, steer the electrons in every electron microscope and in the measuring machine this project is working towards. The whole of chapters 2 to 8 rests on one question that we answer in this chapter for the simplest case: where does a single electron go when we know the fields?

We first meet the parts. At the left of Figure 1.1 the cathode C, a metal electrode, lets electrons escape from its surface (in Thomson's tube a plate in a rarefied gas, from which the discharge itself pulled them; in a television tube a heated strip). Our model starts the electron at rest at the cathode, however it got out. A little way along, a plate with a slit, the anode A, is held at a positive voltage Va​ relative to the cathode, so the electrons are pulled towards it, pass through the slit and carry on in the dark as a thin beam. They fly between two parallel metal plates of length l, a distance d apart, which we can connect to a battery, so that a voltage Vp​ makes an electric field between them. Two coils outside the glass can add a magnetic field over the same stretch. At the far end a screen coated with a phosphor glows where the electrons arrive, and a ruler on the glass reads the position of the spot. Thomson's plates were about 5 cm long, 2 cm broad and 1.5 cm apart, and he read the spot's position from a scale pasted on the tube; we take plates with the same l and d.

Three results will come out of this chapter, and each one is used later. First, the force law that tells an electron what a given electric and magnetic field do to it, derived from a Lagrangian so that it holds at any speed and in any field shape. Second, the energy relation that tells us how fast an electron is after falling through a voltage; the gun of chapter 3 is this relation. Third, a numerical integrator that follows the electron through fields too complicated for pencil and paper, whose errors we measure against an exact solution; chapter 4 uses it to trace rays through lenses.

1.2The model and where it holds

We keep only what makes the tube a tube. The electron is a point particle with charge q=−e and rest mass m; we write e=1.602176634×10−19 C and m=9.10938370×10−31 kg (CODATA 2018). The electric field E and the magnetic field B are given and do not change in time. The beam is so thin that its electrons do not push on each other, so one electron stands for all. The tube is empty: Thomson needed a very good vacuum because stray gas, made conducting by the beam, shorted out the field between his plates and the spot crept back to the middle, a behaviour he describes in his paper.

Between the plates the field is uniform, E=Vp​/d, and zero outside; behind the anode of the gun the field is uniform as well, E=Va​/xa​ for 0<x<xa​. Real plates have fringe fields at their edges, and for plates with d/l=0.3 these reach well into the gap. This is the largest simplification of the tube model. This project does not solve Laplace's equation numerically anywhere (chapter 4 uses an analytic lens field), so the fringe fields stay an omission that we name; here the simplification keeps the algebra visible.

Three numbers tell us whether the simplest physics will do; each is computed for the tube at Va​=2000 V.

  • Relativity. Falling through Va​ it gains the energy eVa​, which is ϵ=eVa​/mc2=0.00391 of its rest energy, and it flies at v/c=0.08822. Relativity is a small correction here (§1.5) but not a negligible one at the 30 kV of a column, where ϵ=0.0587 and v/c=0.328.
  • Radiation. A charge with acceleration a radiates the power P=e2a2/(6πε0​c3) (Larmor; Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, ch. 14). Between the plates a=eE/m=1.17 × 10¹⁵ m/s², so P=7.85 × 10⁻²⁴ W. In the t=1.89 × 10⁻⁹ s that the electron spends there it radiates a fraction 4.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ of its kinetic energy. We ignore radiation.
  • Classical paths. The wavelength of the electron, λ=2.74 × 10⁻¹¹ m (§1.5), is 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ of the plate gap. As long as the fields change over distances much larger than λ, the wave packet follows the classical path. We use classical mechanics.

Two more numbers describe the geometry. The gyroradius in the balancing field of §1.3 is rL​=0.599 m, 12.0 times the plate length, so the magnetic bend over the plates is small; in the 4 mT solenoid of §1.7 it is a few millimetres and the electron circles visibly.

1.3Slow electrons: the pencil-and-paper version

A ball thrown across a room falls along a parabola; a ball tied to a string and swung overhead goes round in a circle; a swimmer pushed by a cross-current and swimming against it at the right speed goes straight. The electron in the tube does all three.

We work with Newton's law mdv/dt=F and the force on a charge q in electric and magnetic fields, the Lorentz force F=q(E+v×B), which §1.4 derives and generalises. For the electron q=−e. Let x point along the tube, y towards the upper plate and z out of the page, so v=(vx​,vy​,0).

An electric field: the parabola

Between the plates the field points along y, E=(0,−E,0) with E=Vp​/d, because the field points from the positive plate to the negative one and we call the upper plate positive for Vp​>0. The force on the electron is F=−eE=(0,+eE,0): it is pushed towards the positive plate, which is what Thomson saw. The force has no x component, so vx​ stays at the entrance value v0​, and the time spent between the plates is t=x/v0​ after a distance x. Along y the acceleration is a=eE/m and the electron starts with vy​=0, so

y(x)=21​at2=2mv02​eE​x2,tanθ=vx​vy​​=mv02​eEl​
(1.1)

The first equation is a parabola, the second gives the angle θ of the path against the axis as the electron leaves the plates after the length l. Behind the plates there is no force, and the electron flies on in a straight line. A line with slope tanθ that touches the parabola at x=l meets the axis at x=l−y(l)/y′(l)=l−21​l=l/2: the electron seems to come from the centre of the plates (checked by SymPy, D5a). With a distance L from the plate end to the screen the spot is therefore at

ys​=(21​l+L)tanθ,L=xs​−xp​−l.
(1.2)

A magnetic field: the circle

With only a magnetic field B=(0,0,−Bp​), pointing into the page for Bp​>0, the force −ev×B is at right angles to v at every instant. A force at right angles to the velocity changes the direction but not the length of v: the speed v stays constant. The electron therefore moves on a circle, held on it by a centripetal force. A circle of radius r at speed v needs the force mv2/r; the magnetic force is evB; equating,

rL​=eBmv​,Ω=rL​v​=meB​,f=2πΩ​.
(1.3)

rL​ is the gyroradius (or Larmor radius), Ω the cyclotron angular frequency. The time for one turn, 2π/Ω, does not depend on the speed, only on B: a fast electron makes a big circle and a slow one a small circle in the same time. Over the plates the electron turns by the angle φ with sinφ=l/rL​; for l≪rL​ this gives φ≈eBl/(mv0​).

Both fields: Thomson's measurement of e/m

The electric force on the electron points towards the positive plate; for our orientation of B the magnetic force points the other way. If the two are equal, eE=evB, the beam goes straight on. That fixes the speed, v0​=E/B, without our knowing e or m separately. Insert it into the angle (1.1) with tanθ≈θ:

θ=me​v02​El​=me​EB2l​⟹me​=B2lθE​.
(1.4)

Every quantity on the right can be measured with a ruler, a voltmeter and an ammeter: the deflection θ of the spot with the field off, the field E=Vp​/d, and the magnetic field B that brings the spot back to the axis. This is Thomson's second method (§1.9); his equation m/e=H2l/(Fθ) is (1.4) written upside down, with his H and F for B and E.

Example 1.1 · the default tube

Take Va​=2000 V, Vp​=100 V, d=15 mm, l=50 mm. Non-relativistically the electron leaves the gun with v0​=(2eVa​/m)1/2=2.652 × 10⁷ m/s; the relativistic value of §1.5 is 2.645 × 10⁷ m/s, which we use from here on. The field is E=Vp​/d=6667 V/m, the acceleration a=eE/m=1.173 × 10¹⁵ m/s², the time in the plates t=l/v0​=1.891 × 10⁻⁹ s, the sideways speed at the exit vy​=at=2.217 × 10⁶ m/s and the displacement there 21​at2=0.002096 m. The angle follows from (1.1), tanθ=0.08382, and with L=xs​−xp​−l=0.19 m the spot is at ys​=0.01802 m by (1.2). The solver of §1.8, which integrates the full relativistic equation of motion, puts the spot at ys​=0.01795 m. The gap of 0.39 % is not a numerical error. It is the Lorentz factor γ=1.00391 of §1.5: the sideways momentum grows as py​=eEt while px​=γmvx​ stays put, so tanθ=eEl/(γmv2), with v the relativistic speed. That gives tanθ=0.08350 and a spot at ys​=0.01795 m, within 1.577 × 10⁻⁴ % of the solver.

The balancing field is B=E/v0​=2.521 × 10⁻⁴ T. The computed spot with that field on is at ys​=1.58 × 10⁻⁸ µm, zero to the resolution of the integration.

1.4From Newton to a Lagrangian★

Newton's law with the Lorentz force is enough for the slow electron of §1.3. It stops being enough in two places. The electron of a 30 kV column moves at a third of the speed of light, where 21​mv2 is no longer its energy. And the magnetic lenses of chapter 4 are not uniform fields: there the vector potential of the field, not only the field itself, decides what is conserved. A Lagrangian handles both, so we derive the force law from one. The passage is marked ★ because it is the heavier algebra of the chapter; (1.8) and (1.7), with their meaning, are all a reader needs from it.

The free particle

Hamilton's principle says that the path a particle takes between two events is the one for which the action S=∫Ldt does not change to first order when the path is varied; the function L is the Lagrangian. For a free particle the only quantity that all observers, however they move, agree on along a path is the proper time τ, the time shown by a clock carried with the particle. Its increment is dτ=dt(1−v2/c2)1/2=dt/γ with γ=(1−v2/c2)−1/2. The simplest action built from it is S=−mc2∫dτ (Landau and Lifshitz, The Classical Theory of Fields, §8; Jackson ch. 12), hence

L0​=−γmc2​=−mc21−c2v2​​.
(1.5)

For v≪c the square root is 1−v2/2c2−v4/8c4−…, so L0​≈−mc2+21​mv2: up to a constant that does not influence the motion, the kinetic energy of Newton. The momentum conjugate to the velocity is ∂L0​/∂vi​. With ∂(v2)/∂vi​=2vi​,

∂vi​∂L0​​=−mc2⋅21​(1−c2v2​)−1/2⋅(−c22vi​​)=γmvi​,

the relativistic momentum p=γmv.

Adding the fields

A charge q in an electrostatic potential φ has the potential energy qφ, which enters L with a minus sign just as V does in L=T−V. The magnetic field enters through the vector potential A, defined by B=∇×A, together with E=−∇φ−∂A/∂t. The two terms −qφ+qv⋅A are the time-and-space components of one four-vector product −q∫Aμ​dxμ, the only invariant that is linear in the potentials (Jackson §12.1; Landau and Lifshitz §16). We adopt it as the form of the interaction, and we test it by its consequences in the next subsection, which must give the Lorentz force and nothing else:

L=−γmc2​−qφ+qv⋅A,q=−e.
(1.6)

The canonical momentum, the derivative of L with respect to the velocity, is the free-particle momentum plus a term from the field:

Key result · canonical momentum
p=∂v∂L​=γmv+qA.
(1.7)

The part γmv is the kinetic momentum: it is what a collision would transfer. The part qA belongs to the field, and it depends on the choice of gauge (adding the gradient of any function to A does not change B). Chapter 4 will use p, not γmv, where a symmetry of the lens fixes a conserved quantity.

The Euler–Lagrange equation gives the Lorentz force

Hamilton's principle becomes, coordinate by coordinate, the Euler–Lagrange equation dtd​∂vx​∂L​=∂x∂L​ (the same equation as in the pendulum note of the simulations part of this site, derived there by varying the path). We write out the x component. The left side needs the time derivative of γmvx​+qAx​. Ax​ depends on the position, which changes along the path, and on time directly, so the chain rule gives dtdAx​​=∂t∂Ax​​+vx​∂x∂Ax​​+vy​∂y∂Ax​​+vz​∂z∂Ax​​. The right side, the derivative of L with respect to x at fixed velocity, is −q∂x​φ+q(vx​∂x​Ax​+vy​∂x​Ay​+vz​∂x​Az​). Moving the Ax​ term across,

dtd(γmvx​)​=−q∂x∂φ​−q∂t∂Ax​​+q[vy​(∂x∂Ay​​−∂y∂Ax​​)+vz​(∂x∂Az​​−∂z∂Ax​​)].

The terms vx​∂x​Ax​ have cancelled between the two sides. The first two terms on the right are qEx​. The brackets are components of B=∇×A: Bz​=∂x​Ay​−∂y​Ax​ and By​=∂z​Ax​−∂x​Az​, so the last term is q(vy​Bz​−vz​By​)=q(v×B)x​. The y and z components follow by cyclic exchange of the letters.

Key result · the force law of the whole project
dtd(γmv)​=q(E+v×B),q=−e,γ=(1−c2v2​)−1/2.
(1.8)

The rate of change of the relativistic momentum equals the Lorentz force. For v≪c it is Newton's law that §1.3 used. The same steps were repeated for all three components by SymPy (checks D1a and D1b, §1.10).

1.5Energy, and why a magnetic field does no work

The Hamiltonian ★

The Hamiltonian is H=p⋅v−L, the energy expressed through the canonical variables. With (1.7) and (1.6) the term qv⋅A appears once with each sign and drops out:

H=γmv2+γmc2​+qφ=γmc2(c2v2​+γ21​)+qφ=γmc2+qφ,

because 1/γ2=1−v2/c2. The kinetic momentum is γmv=p−qA, and (γmc2)2=m2c4+c2∣γmv∣2 (check D2b), so as a function of the canonical momentum

H(r,p,t)=m2c4+c2∣p−qA∣2​+qφ.
(1.9)

Energy conservation

Hamilton's equations give dH/dt=∂H/∂t: the Hamiltonian changes along the path only through an explicit time dependence of the fields. In the static fields of this chapter there is none, so H is constant. Since H=γmc2+qφ and the electron's charge is −e,

Key result · energy and the gun
(γ−1)mc2−eφ(r)=const⟹γ=1+mc2eV​,v=c1−γ21​​
(1.10)

The second form is for an electron that starts at rest at the cathode, φ=0, and has fallen through the potential difference V: the energy it has gained is exactly eV, and that is the definition of the unit electron volt. The speed follows from γ.

The magnetic field never appears in H=γmc2+qφ, so it cannot change the energy. The reason is also visible in the force: v⋅(qv×B)=0, a force at right angles to the motion does no work (SymPy D3b), and the energy theorem d(γmc2)/dt=v⋅d(γmv)/dt (D3a) then gives d(γmc2)/dt=qE⋅v with no B in it. Think of a stone swung on a string: the string pulls inwards at all times, the stone's speed does not change, the string's tension does no work. A magnetic field is such a string, and the electron's energy is only changed by electric fields. That is why a magnetic lens can focus without changing the beam energy, which chapter 4 exploits.

The non-relativistic limit and the size of the correction

For v≪c the series of γ gives (γ−1)mc2=21​mv2+83​mv4/c2+… (SymPy D4b), so the first term of (1.10) reduces to eV=21​mv2, the vNR​=(2eV/m)1/2 that Example 1.1 used. Write ϵ=eV/mc2. Solving (1.10) for the speed and comparing with vNR​ (D4a):

vNR​v​=1−43​ϵ+3223​ϵ2−…
(1.11)

The non-relativistic speed is therefore too large by about three quarters of ϵ. The wave behaves the same way. With the de Broglie relation λ=h/p and the momentum from (pc)2=T(T+2mc2) for a kinetic energy T=eV,

λ=2meV(1+2mc2eV​)​h​=λNR​(1−41​ϵ+…),λNR​=2meV​h​.
(1.12)
V (kV)ϵ=eV/mc2v/cv/vNR​λ (pm)λ/λNR​
0.1001.96 × 10⁻⁴0.019780.9999122.61.000
0.5009.78 × 10⁻⁴0.044210.999354.830.9998
1.000.001960.062470.998538.760.9995
2.000.003910.088220.997127.400.9990
10.00.01960.19500.985612.200.9951
30.00.05870.32840.95836.9790.9856
1000.1960.54820.87633.7010.9544
Example 1.2 · a 30 kV column

At V=30 kV the electron has γ=1.0587, v=9.844 × 10⁷ m/s, v/c=0.328. The non-relativistic formula gives vNR​=1.027 × 10⁸ m/s, too large by 4.4 %, and λ=6.98 pm. The speed error reaches 1 % at V=6830 V. A deflection angle goes as 1/(γmv2)=1/(pv) (§1.3). A calculation that puts 21​mv2=eV in its place takes pv=2eV, while the true value is pv=p2/(γm)=2eV(1+ϵ/2)/(1+ϵ) with ϵ=eV/mc2, so it underestimates the deflection by the factor (1+ϵ/2)/(1+ϵ): by 2.8 % for the column electron and by 0.19 % for the electron of the 2 kV tube.

1.6Where the fields come from

Three field sources are enough for the tube; chapter 4 adds the lens.

Parallel plates. Two large parallel plates a distance d apart at potential difference V have a potential that rises linearly from one to the other, φ(y)=Vy/d, so E=−∇φ is uniform with magnitude V/d. This is the field of the gun between cathode and anode (V=Va​, d=xa​) and of the deflection plates (V=Vp​). It neglects the edges, where the field leaks out.

A pair of coils. A circular loop of radius R carrying the current I produces on its axis, a distance z from its centre, a field along the axis. The Biot–Savart law says that a length dℓ of the wire contributes dB=μ0​Idℓ/(4πr2) at the distance r=(R2+z2)1/2, at right angles to the line to the point. By symmetry the components at right angles to the axis cancel round the loop; the axial component carries the factor R/r. Integrating round the circumference 2πR, and taking N turns,

B(z)=2(R2+z2)3/2μ0​NIR2​.
(1.13)

Two such coils a distance R apart, with the current in the same sense, form a Helmholtz pair. At the midpoint each coil is R/2 away, and the two add to B=2μ0​NIR2/[2(5R2/4)3/2]:

B=(54​)3/2Rμ0​NI​,dzdB​=dz2d2B​=0 at the midpoint
(1.14)

The first three derivatives of the sum of two terms (1.13) vanish there (SymPy D11a, D11b), so the field is nearly uniform over a central stretch whose length is a sizeable fraction of R. For N=100 turns of radius R=50 mm at I=1 A, (1.14) gives B=0.00180 T; Thomson's coils were of this type, and he calibrated their field with a small coil and a ballistic galvanometer rather than from a formula.

A long solenoid. Ampère's law applied to a long coil with n turns per metre gives a uniform axial field B=μ0​nI inside. The model of §1.7 just sets B∥​ as a number.

In every case the electron model reads the field from a function of position and, in later chapters, from a numerical solution. Textbook for these formulas: Griffiths, Introduction to Electrodynamics, ch. 5.

1.7A uniform axial field: the helix

A ball rolled round the inside of a funnel winds round and round while it moves along the axis. A uniform magnetic field along the tube does the same to an electron that does not start exactly on the axis.

Let the field point along b^, constant in space, with no electric field. By §1.5 the energy stays constant, hence so does γ, and the equation of motion (1.8) for u=γv becomes the linear equation

dtdu​=Ωu×b^,Ω=γmqB​  (negative for the electron).
(1.15)

Split u into the part u∥​ along b^ and the part u⊥​ across it. The cross product has no component along b^, so u∥​ stays constant. Take b^=z^ and combine the two transverse components into one complex number w=ux​+iuy​. Then dw/dt=Ω(uy​−iux​)=−iΩw, whose solution is w=w0​e−iΩt: a vector of fixed length that turns with the angular frequency Ω. In real form, with the electron at the origin at t=0 and γ constant,

u⊥​(t)=u⊥0​cosΩt+(u⊥0​×b^)sinΩt,r(t)=γ1​[u∥​tb^+u⊥0​ΩsinΩt​+(u⊥0​×b^)Ω1−cosΩt​].
(1.16)

Differentiating shows that this solves (1.15) and r˙=u/γ (SymPy D7a, D7b). The transverse motion is a circle through the starting point of radius rL​=∣u⊥0​∣/(γ∣Ω∣) (D7c), which is

Key result · gyroradius and the helix
rL​=eBγmv⊥​​=eBp⊥​​,T=∣Ω∣2π​=eB2πγm​,pitch=v∥​T.
(1.17)

Slow electrons give back (1.3). The relativistic factor γ lengthens the period: a fast electron needs a little longer for a turn. Combined with the steady motion along the field the path is a helix of radius rL​ and pitch v∥​T.

Now send electrons from one point of the axis in slightly different directions, each making a small angle α with the axis. They have almost the same v∥​ and the same period T, whatever their α, so after one turn all of them are back on the axis, at the same distance

L=v∥​T=eB2πγmv∥​​.
(1.18)

This is a lens. Electrons spread out from a point and reunite at another point, because they all need the same time to complete a turn. With Va​=2000 V and B∥​=4 mT, (1.18) gives L=0.2367 m; an electron leaving at α=60 mrad circles with rL​=0.00226 m. Figure 1.3 shows six of them. A real magnetic lens, chapter 4, is a short coil whose field rises and falls along the axis, and it twists the beam by the angle it gains while crossing: this helix is its seed.

1.8Following the electron on a computer: Runge–Kutta and Boris

Pencil and paper solve a uniform field. A lens, a plate with fringe fields or a gun with space charge need a computer that moves the electron a short time step h at a time. Two methods do the work in this project, and they fail in different ways.

The state of the electron is (r,u) with u=γv. (1.8) written for it reads

r˙=γu​,u˙=mq​(E(r)+γu​×B(r)),γ=1+c2∣u∣2​​,
(1.19)

which is the form both integrators advance. We test both against the exact helix of (1.16), because there the right answer is known for every time.

Classical Runge–Kutta (RK4)

For y˙​=f(y) the classical fourth-order step uses four slopes, one at the start, two at the midpoint (the second improved by the first) and one at the end, and combines them with weights 1,2,2,1:

yn+1​=yn​+6h​(k1​+2k2​+2k3​+k4​),k1​=f(yn​), k2​=f(yn​+2h​k1​), k3​=f(yn​+2h​k2​), k4​=f(yn​+hk3​).
(1.20)

Its local error per step is of order h5 and, accumulated over 1/h steps, its global error is of order h4 (Hairer, Nørsett and Wanner, Solving Ordinary Differential Equations I, §II.1 for the order conditions). It needs four evaluations of the fields per step.

What RK4 does to a rotation we can compute exactly, because the magnetic motion is the linear equation w˙=−iΩw. One RK4 step multiplies w by the polynomial of the exponential, R(−iθ)=1−iθ−θ2/2+iθ3/6+θ4/24 with θ=Ωh. The true factor e−iθ has length 1. The length of R is, by expanding (SymPy D10a),

∣R∣2=1−72θ6​+576θ8​,θ−argR=120θ5​−336θ7​+…
(1.21)

The first expression is smaller than 1: every step shrinks the circle a little. The electron loses energy to the method although nothing in the physics takes any. With N=2π/θ steps per turn the loss in n turns is 1−∣R∣2Nn of u⊥2​ (D10b gives the phase error). For N=16 the loss is 0.080 % per turn, and half of u⊥2​ (most of the kinetic energy, since the motion is mostly transverse) is gone after 867 turns. For N=64 it takes 12600 turns to lose 1 %.

The Boris pusher ★

Boris (1970) gave the method that plasma and beam codes still use. It splits the step into what the electric field does, a push, and what the magnetic field does, a rotation. The electric push is applied in two halves, before and after the rotation, which makes the scheme symmetric in time and therefore of second order. The velocity u lives at the half steps and the position at the whole steps (leapfrog), and with a=qh/(2m):

u−=un−1/2​+aE,u′=u−+u−×t,u+=u−+u′×s,un+1/2​=u++aE,
(1.22)

with t=aB/γ−, γ−=(1+∣u−∣2/c2)1/2 and s=2t/(1+t2); then rn+1​=rn​+hun+1/2​/γn+1/2​. The two middle steps are the rotation. We show what they do in the plane normal to B, with t=tz^ and u−=(ux​,uy​). Then u−×t=(uy​t,−ux​t), so u′=(ux​+tuy​, uy​−tux​), and with s=sz^, s=2t/(1+t2),

ux+​=ux​(1−st)+suy​,uy+​=uy​(1−st)−sux​.

Because 1−st=(1−t2)/(1+t2), the pair (1−st, s) is (cosφ,sinφ) with t=tan(φ/2): the two steps turn the vector by exactly the angle φ (SymPy D8c; for t in any direction D8a shows the same with Rodrigues' rotation formula). A rotation does not change a length, so ∣u+∣=∣u−∣ exactly (D8b). The true angle per step is Ωh; Boris turns by φ=2arctan(Ωh/2), which differs by

Ωh−2arctan2Ωh​=12(Ωh)3​−80(Ωh)5​+…
(1.23)

per step (D9b). That is a phase error: the electron goes round slightly too slowly, and the error grows with the number of turns, of order h2 in all. The energy is another matter. In a pure magnetic field the rotation keeps ∣u∣ exactly, so the energy does not drift however many turns are computed. The position update uses the chord hv, not the arc, so the path is a regular polygon with turning angle φ and chord hv=(Ωh)rL​; the polygon's circumscribed circle has radius chord/2sin(φ/2), that is

rBoris​=rL​1+(2Ωh​)2​
(1.24)

(D9a). The radius is off by a fixed fraction and does not drift: 1.0191 of rL​ at 16 steps per turn, 1.0012 at 64. With an electric field present the energy is not exactly constant, but the error stays bounded and does not grow in time; Qin and co-workers (Physics of Plasmas 20, 084503, 2013) show that the Boris step preserves phase-space volume, which is the usual explanation for this long-term behaviour; volume preservation alone does not prove it.

Both against the exact helix

We start an electron of V=2 kV in B=10 mT at χ=1.2 rad to the field, so that it circles with rL​=0.01407 m, and follow it for 20 turns of period T=3.586 × 10⁻⁹ s with N steps per turn. The table gives the distance between computed and exact position after 20 turns in units of rL​ and the relative change of the kinetic energy over the run (for RK4 the loss, for Boris the signed noise). The "predicted" columns are not fits: the Boris phase error accumulated over 20N steps is 20N(θ−2arctan2θ​), the RK4 one 20N(θ−argR), and the RK4 energy loss is sin2χ(1−(∣R∣2)20N) from (1.21) (only the transverse part of u shrinks).

NBoris, errorBoris, predictedRK4, errorRK4, predictedRK4 energyRK4 energy, predictedBoris energy
161.451.420.02150.02350.01370.0137noise
320.4010.3990.001440.001544.39 × 10⁻⁴4.39 × 10⁻⁴noise
640.1010.1019.31 × 10⁻⁵9.69 × 10⁻⁵1.38 × 10⁻⁵1.38 × 10⁻⁵noise
1280.02520.02525.92 × 10⁻⁶6.07 × 10⁻⁶4.31 × 10⁻⁷4.31 × 10⁻⁷noise
2560.006310.006313.74 × 10⁻⁷3.80 × 10⁻⁷1.35 × 10⁻⁸1.35 × 10⁻⁸noise
5120.001580.001582.34 × 10⁻⁸2.37 × 10⁻⁸4.21 × 10⁻¹⁰4.21 × 10⁻¹⁰noise

The position error of Boris falls with slope −2.00 in logN (between N=64 and 256), as h2 predicts; the RK4 error falls with slope −3.98, as h4 predicts; the RK4 energy error falls with slope −5.00, one power faster than the position error, as (1.21) predicts. The energy of Boris stays at the noise of 64-bit arithmetic in every case, the last column. At N=64 the predicted position error of Boris is within 0.12 % of the measured one, and the prediction improves with N; for RK4 the prediction is within about ten per cent at the smallest N and closer at larger N, because its total error is not only phase error.

Key result · which to use

RK4 is much more accurate per step: at N=64 its error is 9.31 × 10⁻⁵ of rL​, against 0.101 for Boris. But RK4 loses energy steadily, at a rate set by Ωh. Boris uses one field evaluation per step instead of four, keeps the energy and the radius bounded however long it runs, and its error is a phase error that does not distort the shape of the orbit. We use RK4 for short paths where accuracy counts and Boris for the many-turn paths of later chapters, and we check each result against the other.

Example 1.3 · the same work

RK4 at N=16 uses 64 field evaluations per turn; Boris at N=64 uses 64. At that equal cost the RK4 error after 20 turns is 0.0215 of rL​ and the Boris error 0.101: RK4 is ahead in position. It has paid for it with 1.37 % of its energy; Boris none.

1.9Thomson's tube, simulated and compared with Thomson's data

The simulation at the end of the chapter follows the electron of §1.8 through uniform fields, with every symbol of the chapter a slider. With B at zero and E at the value of the worked example the path is the parabola of Figure 1.2. With E at zero and the velocity at a right angle to B it is the circle; at a small angle to B, the helix of §1.7. With E=vB and a right angle between them the electron goes straight on, Thomson's balance. The integrator and its time step are sliders too, so the errors of §1.8 can be provoked by hand: a step of a tenth of a period makes the energy error of RK4 visible within a few turns.

The method recovers e/m from the simulation

We repeat Thomson's second method on the computer. The deflection with only the electric field is measured on the path after the plates; the magnetic field that brings the spot back to the axis is B=E/v0​=2.521 × 10⁻⁴ T; and (1.4) gives e/m=θE/(B2l)=1.7479 × 10¹¹ C/kg, from the angle θ=0.08330 rad of the simulated path. The value the simulation was run with is e/m=1.7588 × 10¹¹ C/kg. The method returns it to 0.62 %. The deficit has a known cause, and it is the physics of §1.5 showing through. (1.4) assumes a small angle and a non-relativistic electron. With the relativistic momentum the angle of the path is θ=arctan(eEl/(γmv2)), as in §1.3 after the correction for γ. So the measured θ is smaller than eEl/mv2 by two factors: the electron is heavier by γ=1.00391, which costs 1/γ=0.99610; and an angle is smaller than its tangent y=0.08350, which costs arctany/y=0.99769. Their product 0.99380 matches the measured ratio 0.99380 to 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁴. Multiplying the inferred value by γ alone brings the ratio to 0.99769, and the remainder is the arctangent.

Thomson's own numbers

The 1897 paper (J. J. Thomson, Philosophical Magazine 44, 293) gives two tables of m/e in CGS electromagnetic units, from two methods. The first measures the energy the beam deposits on a thermocouple and the charge it brings into a cylinder, and the radius of its path in a magnetic field; it gives m/e=I2Q/2W with I=Hρ. The second is the crossed-field method of §1.3. We typed in all 26 rows of the first table and all 7 of the second, from the transcription of C. J. Giunta (Le Moyne College) of the original, converted them to SI (1 g/abC=10−4 kg/C), and plot e/m in Figure 1.5 (data and provenance: data/ch01/thomson1897.json).

The result is a plain statement of how far an early measurement lies from the modern one. The first method gives e/m between 0.57 and 1.78 times CODATA, with a mean of 1.19 (tubes 1 and 2: 1.26; tube 3: 0.67). The second method gives 0.38 to 0.52 times CODATA, mean 0.45: the value of e/m is too small by a factor of about two. In his text Thomson says that he judges the first-method values for tubes 1 and 2 too large in e/m, because charge leaks from the inner cylinder through the conducting gas, and that the uncertainty of the radius ρ alone is about 20 per cent. The data show the first part: tubes 1 and 2 lie above CODATA, tube 3 below. Thomson names a cause for the second method himself, right after his second table: the coils' field outside the plates points the other way and bends the rays back, so the effective magnetic field is smaller than the value he used, his m/e comes out too large and his e/m too small. We have not modelled that reversed field; it, and the non-uniform field over the plates (§1.2), are the likely parts of the factor of two. The point that the paper does support is the one he drew: all gases and electrode metals give the same m/e, of order 10−7 in his units, about a thousandth of 10−4, the smallest value known before, that of the hydrogen ion in electrolysis. He notes that the smallness of m/e may come from a small m or a large e, and argues from Lenard's measurements that the carriers are small compared with ordinary molecules.

Our simulation recovers e/m because it contains none of the things that troubled the experiment: no gas, a perfectly uniform field, no uncertainty in the field's strength or the beam's path. Comparing a model with data teaches something only where the two differ by more than the data's own scatter. Thomson's rows of the first method spread over a factor 3.1, and the second method sits a factor of two from the truth, against the 0.62 % deficit of the idealised model, which has a known cause. We also checked Thomson's arithmetic. His columns obey m/e=I2Q/2W in all rows of the first table but one, with a median deviation of 1.4 % and a largest deviation of 8.1 %, the size of the rounding of a one- or two-digit entry. In one row (hydrogen, tube 1, W/Q printed as 6×1012) the printed W/Q disagrees by a factor of 9.99 with the same row's m/e and v; the m/e and v agree with W/Q=6×1011, so the transcription or the original has a misprint in that cell. We used the printed m/e column throughout.

The numbers of the chapter were checked the other way round. The module of the page, physics/ch01.js, and an independent NumPy implementation, ref/ch01.py, are run on the same cases by checks/check_parity.py, and every number quoted in the prose is computed by both (checks/check_numbers.py): the printed strings must be identical. The two are float64 and use the same algorithm, so what remains is rounding. The energy change of a run is a difference of two nearly equal numbers; it is compared with an absolute floor that the module states, and every other output agrees to rounding.

1.11What the model leaves out, and what we pass on

The model has a short list of things it does not contain. Fringe fields of the plates (§1.2): the largest error of the tube model; a field solver would repair it, and this project names it as an omission (chapter 4 uses an analytic lens field). Space charge: electrons repel each other, and at the currents of an electron column the repulsion widens the beam; chapter 5 returns to it. The source: the electron here starts at rest from a point; a real cathode emits a spread of energies and directions, and chapter 2 describes them. Spin and radiation: negligible here, with 4.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ of the energy radiated. Gas: a vacuum. The next, more complete model for an electron in given fields is a field solver for E,B from the electrodes and coils (finite or boundary elements), with the same pusher; it is outside this project.

Hand-over to chapter 2

Chapter 2 receives from this chapter: (1) the force law (1.8) with q=−e, the one equation that moves every electron in the project; (2) the energy relation (1.10), so that an electron that starts at rest at a surface and falls through V has γ=1+eV/mc2, which chapter 3 turns into the gun; (3) the Boris and RK4 steppers of physics/ch01.js, with the measured error laws of §1.8, to follow electrons through any given field; (4) the helix (1.16) as the seed of the magnetic lens of chapter 4. Chapter 2 supplies the other end of the column: how many electrons leave the tip per second, with what spread of energy, from how small a spot. The electron of this chapter, that leaves a point at rest, becomes there a stream with a current and a brightness.

Problems
  1. Show that the straight line leaving the plates, traced backwards, meets the axis at the centre of the plates (SymPy D5a does it; do it by hand from (1.1)).
  2. For which anode voltage does the relativistic speed fall 1 % below the non-relativistic one? (Solve v/vNR​≈1−43​ϵ=0.99; the exact answer of the code is 6830 V.)
  3. Show that u+ in (1.22) has the same length as u− for an arbitrary direction of t, starting from ∣u′∣2=∣u−∣2(1+t2) when u−⊥t.
  4. An electron of 30 kV in a field of 1 mT has rL​=0.593 m (use (1.17)). How many field evaluations per turn does Boris need to keep its radius within 0.1 % of rL​ ((1.24))? Answer: at least 70.2 steps, which is rounded up to the next whole number.

Chapter 2The source

The chapter starts at the metal. It derives the barrier an electron meets outside a tungsten surface (applied field and image charge), the probability of tunnelling through it (WKB), the supply of electrons from the Fermi–Dirac gas, and from the three the Fowler–Nordheim, Richardson–Dushman and Schottky formulas, the energy spread and the reduced brightness of each source. It then follows the vacuum physics (Hertz–Knudsen flux, coverage kinetics, flash cleaning) that makes a cold tip bright and fragile at once. A published tungsten-tip data set and a published measurement of current decay against pressure are laid over the model and the differences are stated. Four numbers go to chapter 3: emission current, reduced brightness, energy spread, virtual source size. Assumed, not measured: the field factor k, the work functions, the desorption energy and the effect of an adsorbate; each is a control of the simulation.

2.1A needle, a wall and a leak

Every electron beam in this project starts at a piece of metal. We want to know what that piece of metal has to look like, what is applied to it, and what comes out, in numbers the next chapters can use.

Anyone who has touched a door handle on a dry winter day has met the main idea. The spark jumps from a fingertip and not from the flat of the hand, and a lightning rod is a pointed rod and not a plate. Charge on a conductor crowds where the surface curves sharply, and the electric field next to the surface grows with that crowding. A needle tip is the extreme case: a few tens of nanometres across, it turns a modest voltage into a field that is enormous on the scale of atoms.

2.1.1Work function and the wall

Inside a metal the conduction electrons fill states up to an energy called the Fermi level. We take that level as the zero of energy in this chapter. An electron at the Fermi level is not free: to take it to rest just outside the surface costs a definite energy, the work function φ. We picture a bowl of water whose surface is the Fermi level and whose rim is φ higher; φ is the height of the rim above the water. For clean tungsten we use φ=4.5 eV, the value Dolan and Dyke called "the accepted average value for clean tungsten" in 1954. One electronvolt is 1.602176634×10−19 J. We shall treat φ as a parameter that can be changed, because the whole story of this chapter depends on how sensitive the current is to it.

There are three ways to get an electron over or through the rim. Heat the metal until enough electrons have the energy to climb it (thermionic emission). Apply a field that lowers the rim a little (Schottky emission). Or apply a field so strong that the rim becomes a thin wall and the electrons tunnel through it (field emission). The cold source that Applied Materials describes publicly for its electron-beam metrology column is of the third kind; the Schottky source of the second kind is its main competitor. The three are one calculation, and we do it once.

2.1.2The field at the apex

Take a conducting sphere of radius r carrying charge Q and held at potential V relative to far away. Outside it the potential is that of a point charge, Q/(4πε0​ρ) at distance ρ from the centre, so V=Q/(4πε0​r). The field at the surface is Q/(4πε0​r2), and eliminating Q gives F=V/r. A real tip is a sphere sitting on a cone or a wire, with an anode at a finite distance, and the shank takes some of the potential drop. This is folded into one dimensionless factor k, of order unity to several, so that

F=krV​(2.1)

with k=1 for the isolated sphere. The value k=5 is used for tungsten tips by Chapman (1971) and by Ayari et al. (2023), whose data we use in section 2.9; we take it as an assumption, and the chapter says where it enters.

Example 2.1 · The field at a tip

A tip of radius r=50 nm at V=1000 V with k=5 has F=1000/(5×50×10−9)=4.00×109 V/m=4.0 V/nm. For scale, the field of a proton at one Bohr radius is 5.14×1011 V/m, so this is 1/129 of the field inside a hydrogen atom: a field that changes the energy of an electron by 4.0 eV over each nanometre. An electron at the Fermi level, in this field, has to climb a wall of height φ that falls by eF per unit length, which would reach the Fermi level after φ/(eF)=1.125 nm. That is the thickness of the wall it must tunnel through, a few atomic diameters.

Key result · the field of a needle

F=V/(kr): halving the radius doubles the field at the same voltage. With r in nanometres and a kilovolt applied, fields of several volts per nanometre are reached.

2.2The wall an electron sees

Outside the metal, an electron feels two things: the applied field, which pulls it away from the surface, and its own image, which pulls it back. We add the two energies.

2.2.1The image force

Put an electron at distance x from the plane surface of a conductor. The conduction electrons rearrange until the field just outside the surface is perpendicular to it. For the region outside the metal this arrangement is exactly what a single positive charge +e at distance x inside the metal, the mirror image of the electron, would produce. The force on the electron is therefore that of a charge +e at distance 2x:

Fim​(x)=−4πε0​(2x)2e2​=−16πε0​x2e2​(2.2)

The potential energy is minus the work needed to take the electron from x out to infinity against this attraction,

Uim​(x)=−∫x∞​16πε0​x′2e2​dx′=−16πε0​xe2​(2.3)

(One might expect e2/(8πε0​x), the energy of the real pair at separation 2x. It is twice as large, because as the electron moves away the induced charge in the metal rearranges, and only half of the pair's energy is stored in the field outside the surface. Integrating the force, as above, takes this into account.)

2.2.2The Schottky–Nordheim barrier

The applied field F, directed so that it pulls electrons out, contributes −eFx. Measuring all energies from the Fermi level, an electron at the Fermi level sees outside the surface

U(x)=φ−eFx−16πε0​xe2​(2.4)

This is the Schottky–Nordheim (SN) barrier. For F=0 it is the work function wall rounded off by the image force. For F>0 it falls linearly and is cut by the image term near the surface. Writing Q0​=e2/(16πε0​), the energy U is zero where eFx2−φx+Q0​=0, that is at

x1,2​=2eFφ​(1∓1−f​),f=φ24eFQ0​​=4πε0​φ2e3F​(2.5)

The dimensionless number f is the scaled field. The barrier exists as long as f<1; at f=1 the two roots merge and the top of the barrier touches the Fermi level. The field at which this happens, FR​=4πε0​φ2/e3, is 14.06 V/nm for φ=4.5 eV, so f=F/FR​. Setting dU/dx=0 gives the top of the barrier at xm​=Q0​/(eF)​, where Umax​=φ−Δφ with the Schottky lowering

Δφ=4πε0​e3F​​=φf​,Δφ=1.2000 eV×F/(V/nm)​(2.6)

The derivation of x1,2​, of f, and of Δφ was checked symbolically (checks C1 and C2 in section 2.13).

Example 2.2 · The barrier at F = 4 V/nm

Here f=0.2844, the roots are x1​=0.087 nm and x2​=1.038 nm, and the top of the barrier is Δφ=2.40 eV below the zero-field rim, at 2.10 eV above the Fermi level. A Fermi-level electron meets a barrier x2​−x1​=1.04−0.087≈0.95 nm wide.

Where the model is not trusted. The image term diverges at the surface, and at x1​ of less than a tenth of a nanometre the picture of a smooth classical image charge is no longer meaningful. The standard treatment, which we follow, simply uses the barrier between its two roots; the fact that the result depends only on the region x1​<x<x2​, where the barrier is above the electron, hides the problem. It is one of the reasons the current in section 2.9 is predicted only to a factor, not to a percent.

2.3Leaking through: the WKB transmission

A wave that meets a barrier higher than its energy does not stop at the edge. Inside the barrier it dies away exponentially, and what is left at the far side leaves as an electron. We now compute how much is left.

Let an electron approach the surface with energy w of motion normal to it. We write the time-independent Schrödinger equation for that motion,

−2mℏ2​ψ′′(x)+U(x)ψ(x)=wψ(x)(2.7)

In the barrier, U>w, so ψ′′=κ2ψ with κ(x)=2m(U(x)−w)​/ℏ. If κ were constant the solution that decays towards larger x would be e−κx. When κ varies slowly, ∣dκ/dx∣≪κ2, the WKB approximation replaces κx by ∫κdx:

ψ(x)≈ψ(x1​)exp(−∫x1​x​κ(x′)dx′)(2.8)

The probability of finding the electron, ∣ψ∣2, falls by the square of that factor between the two turning points x1​ and x2​. The transmission probability is taken as this ratio:

D(w)≈e−G(w),G(w)=ℏ2​∫x1​x2​​2m(U(x)−w)​dx(2.9)

The approximation fails close to the turning points, where κ→0, so D is only reliable when G is large, and the prefactor that belongs to the exact solution is dropped; for the barriers that give currents we care about, G is of order 10 (the exponent in Example 2.3 is 10.7) and the missing prefactor is a factor of order one that is absorbed in the uncertainty named in section 2.9. Allaham et al. (2022) give the same step in their equations (3) and (4), with the constant 2κe​=10.246 eV−1/2nm−1 which is 22m(1eV)​/ℏ; we recomputed it.

2.3.1The triangular barrier

Without the image term the barrier is U=φ−eFx, which meets the Fermi level (w=0) at x=φ/(eF). Then

G△​=ℏ2​∫0φ/eF​2m(φ−eFx)​dx=3ℏe42m​​Fφ3/2​≡bFφ3/2​(2.10)

The integral is 32​φ3/2/(eF) times 2m​ times 2/ℏ. The constant b=42m​/(3ℏe) is the second Fowler–Nordheim constant; it equals 6.8309 eV−3/2Vnm−1 (Forbes quotes 6.830 890; check C3). In words: G grows as the wall gets higher (φ3/2) and shrinks as the field gets stronger (1/F). With the example numbers G△​=16.30.

2.3.2With the image term: the function v(f) ★

With the image term, U−w=eF(x−x1​)(x2​−x)/x between the roots (the roots depend on the energy through φ−w in place of φ). We put x=x1​+(x2​−x1​)sin2ϑ with 0≤ϑ≤π/2, so that (x−x1​)(x2​−x)=Δ2sin2ϑcos2ϑ, dx=2Δsinϑcosϑdϑ, Δ=x2​−x1​:

G=ℏ22m​​eF​∫0π/2​x1​+Δsin2ϑ​2Δ2sin2ϑcos2ϑ​dϑ≡bFφ3/2​v(f)(2.11)

which has no singularity and is evaluated by Gauss–Legendre quadrature in ref/ch02.py and physics/ch02.js (48 points for the exponent at a single energy, 64 for v(f), 24 inside the energy integral of section 2.4). The right-hand side defines v(f), a correction factor that depends only on f: it equals 1 for f→0 (no image term) and falls to 0 at f=1, where the barrier has disappeared. In the older literature it is written with the elliptic integrals of Nordheim; Forbes (2006) found that v≈1−f+61​flnf is good to 0.0024 everywhere on 0≤f≤1. Our quadrature agrees: the largest difference on a grid of 199 values is 0.00238 (check C7).

v(f)≈1−f+6f​lnf(2.12)

For the working point, v=0.6538 by quadrature and 0.6560 from the approximation.

Example 2.3 · The transmission at the working point

G=bφ3/2v/F=16.30×0.6538=10.66 and D=e−G=2.35×10−5. The image force changes G from 16.30 to 10.66 and therefore multiplies the transmission by e16.30−10.66=283. Of every 42532 electrons that arrive at the wall one gets out.

2.4Counting the electrons that arrive: the supply function

The transmission is a probability per electron. To get a current we need to know how many electrons strike the surface per second, with which normal energy, and that is a count in the metal.

We treat the conduction electrons as a gas of free particles with the Fermi–Dirac occupation F(E)=[1+e(E−μ)/kT]−1, with μ=0 the Fermi level. A momentum cell of size d3p holds 2d3p/h3 electron states (the 2 is the spin). Electrons with velocity component vx​ normal to the surface, directed at it, reach unit area of surface per unit time at the rate vx​ times their density. So the current density of electrons that arrive with the momenta in d3p is

dJin​=eh32​F(E)vx​d3p(2.13)

Split E=w+εt​ into the normal energy w=px2​/2m and the transverse energy εt​=(py2​+pz2​)/2m. Then vx​dpx​=dw, and the transverse momentum element is dpy​dpz​=πd(pt2​)=2πmdεt​. A fraction D(w) of what arrives is transmitted. Adding up,

J=e∫dwD(w)h34πm​∫0∞​F(w+εt​)dεt​=e∫N(w)D(w)dw(2.14)

(spin 2 times 2πm gives 4πm). The inner integral is elementary, because ∫w∞​FdE=kTln(1+e−w/kT). It defines the supply function, the number of electrons per unit area, time and energy that arrive with normal energy w:

N(w)=h34πmkT​ln(1+e−w/kT)(2.15)

The check C4 verifies the derivative that defines it. For w≪−kT, N→4πm(−w)/h3: at low temperature the number of arriving electrons grows linearly with how far below the Fermi level they sit, and N drops to zero above it on a scale kT.

Key result · the master formula of this chapter

J=e∫N(w)D(w)dw, with N from (2.15) and the transmission from (2.9), which the code evaluates as D=1/(1+eG): equal to e−G wherever G is large, and bounded by 1 near the top. Above the barrier top, where there are no turning points, the code continues G linearly in energy with the slope it has 0.02 eV below the top (a parabolic-top continuation in the spirit of Kemble), so D rises smoothly to 1. Fowler–Nordheim, Richardson–Dushman and Schottky emission are three limits of it; the code of this page evaluates it numerically, without limits, wherever it needs to.

One assumption is hidden here and we state it: D depends only on the energy w of the normal motion, not on εt​. That holds for a plane, smooth surface in an isotropic free-electron metal. It fails for a real crystal face, where the band structure and the surface potential differ from face to face (this is why different tungsten planes emit differently).

2.5The Fowler–Nordheim equation

At low temperature the master formula can be done by hand. The result is the equation that the experimenters of the 1950s used to count nothing but volts and amperes.

2.5.1Linearising the exponent

At T→0 only electrons with w<0 exist and N=4πm(−w)/h3. Because D=e−G changes so fast with w, only energies within a fraction of an electronvolt of the Fermi level matter, and we expand G there to first order:

G(w)≈GF​−dw​,d1​=−dwdG​​w=0​(2.16)

with GF​=G(0), the exponent computed in section 2.3. The slope: raising w by a small amount lowers the barrier height seen from the electron by the same amount. Because the image term does not depend on w, that is the same as lowering φ at fixed F, so dG/dw=−∂G/∂φ. With G=bφ3/2v(f)/F and f∝φ−2 (so df/dφ=−2f/φ),

∂φ∂G​=Fb​[23​φ1/2v−2fφ3/2φv′​]=2F3bφ​​t(f),t(f)≡v−34​fv′(f)(2.17)

For the triangular barrier v=1, t=1, and d=2F/(3bφ​)=ℏeF/(22mφ​), which is the decay length of the electron's states in energy: d is an energy, 0.184 eV at the working point for the triangular barrier; with the image term it is divided by t(f) and becomes 0.175 eV. Inserting Forbes' v gives

t(f)≈1+9f​−18f​lnf(2.18)

(check C6 does the algebra symbolically; check C8 confirms ∂G/∂φ numerically by differencing the quadrature of section 2.3: the formula with the exact t agrees to 2.5×10−11, and Forbes' t(f) is 0.32 % off).

2.5.2The integral

At T=0, J=eh34πm​e−GF​∫−∞0​(−w)ew/ddw, and ∫−∞0​(−w)ew/ddw=d2 (integration by parts, check C5). So

J0​=h34πme​d2e−GF​(2.19)

Inserting d=ℏeF/(22mφ​t), ℏ=h/2π, and GF​=bφ3/2v/F, the constants combine (check C5):

J0​=8πhe3​φt2(f)F2​exp(−v(f)Fbφ3/2​)(2.20)
Key result · Fowler–Nordheim equation with the image-charge barrier (Murphy and Good form)

J0​=φa​t2F2​e−vbφ3/2/F, with a=e2/(8πh)=1.5414 μAeVV−2 and b=6.8309 eV−3/2Vnm−1 when φ is in electronvolt and F in volt per nanometre. It follows from the model of sections 2.2 to 2.4 at T=0, with G expanded to first order about the Fermi level, for f away from 1; on this page it is evaluated with Forbes' approximations for v and t.

symbolmeaningvalue or unitwhere it comes from
J0​emitted current density, zero temperatureA/m², here 1.13×108 at F=4 V/nmthe result
e, helementary charge, Planck constantexact SI values2019 SI
Ffield at the emitting surfaceV/m; F=V/(kr)(2.1)
φwork function4.5 eV, tungsten (assumed)input

t(f)prefactor correction v−34​fv′1.0515(2.17), (2.18)
