Dimensional check: e2F2/(hφ) in the units of the table is μAeVV−2⋅(V/nm)2/eV=μA/nm2, a current density. Limiting cases: for F→0 (f→0) v,t→1 and the equation becomes the triangular-barrier form of Fowler and Nordheim (1928); for f→1, v→0 and the exponent no longer suppresses the current. At about f≈0.8 the derivation fails, as Allaham et al. (2022) note: the barrier is then so low and thin that the expansion of G about the Fermi level is poor. Electrons at the Fermi level do not yet fly over it; at f=0.8 its top still lies 0.475 eV above them, and fly-over begins only at f=1.

Example 2.4 · Fowler–Nordheim current density at the working point

At F=4 V/nm and φ=4.5 eV: f=0.2844, Forbes' v=0.6560 (the quadrature gives 0.6538; we use Forbes' value here because the formula is evaluated with it on this page), t=1.0515, bφ3/2/F=16.30. Then J0​=(1.5414×10−6/4.5)×42/1.0512×e−10.69 A/nm², which is 1.13×108 A/m2. The full integral of section 2.4, without any approximation, gives 1.16×108 A/m2, at 300 K.

2.5.3Finite temperature ★

With the linearised D and the full N, the integral is J=e(4πmkT/h3)e−GF​∫ln(1+e−w/kT)ew/ddw. Integrating by parts (the boundary terms vanish for d>kT) turns it into kTd​∫ew/d/(1+ew/kT)dw, and ∫−∞∞​eau/(1+eu)du=π/sinπa for 0<a<1, with u=w/kT and a=kT/d. Hence

J(T)=J0​sin(πkT/d)πkT/d​(2.21)

(check C9 evaluates both sides numerically at 30 digits). At the working point, 300 K, πkT/d=0.464 and the factor is 1.037, a 3.7 % correction. The factor diverges when πkT/d→π, that is when kT→d, and is a poor description well before that: electrons far above the Fermi level, where the barrier is thinner, then dominate and the linearisation of G fails. That is the transition to thermal-field emission; there we integrate numerically.

2.5.4The Fowler–Nordheim plot

Experimenters measure current I at voltage V, not J at F. If the emitting area A is constant and F=V/ζ (so ζ=kr is the voltage conversion length), I=AJ0​ gives

lnV2I​=lnφt2ζ2Aa​−bφ3/2ζVv(f)​(2.22)

Plotted against 1/V, the right-hand side is a straight line to a good approximation. Its slope is d[v(f)/V]/d(1/V) times −bφ3/2ζ, and because f∝V the derivative is v−fv′=s(f). For Forbes' v this is exactly s(f)=1−f/6 (check C6b). So

SFN​=−bφ3/2ζ(1−6f​)(2.23)

A measured slope gives ζ if φ is known, and then r=ζ/k if k is. Section 2.9 does this with real data.

2.6Heat helps: Richardson–Dushman and Schottky emission

Warm the same metal and the supply of energetic electrons in the tail of the Fermi function takes over from tunnelling. The master formula gives that limit in one line.

For electrons with w above the top of the barrier, D≈1, and ln(1+e−w/kT)≈e−w/kT when w≫kT. With no field the top is at w=φ:

J=e∫φ∞​h34πmkT​e−w/kTdw=h34πmek2​T2e−φ/kT≡AR​T2e−φ/kT(2.24)

with AR​=1.20173×106 Am−2K−2 (check C10; the textbook value is 1.2017×106). This is the Richardson–Dushman law. A field lowers the top of the barrier by the Schottky lowering Δφ of (2.6) and the emission is that of a work function φ−Δφ:

J=AR​T2exp(−kTφ−Δφ​)(2.25)

For our Schottky preset we choose φ=2.9 eV for the zirconium-oxide-coated surface (an assumed value; the Hitachi page cited below says only that the coating lowers the work function), T=1800 K, and a field F=0.5 V/nm at the apex (we choose k so that this holds; this is an assumed operating point, not a quoted specification). Then kT=0.155 eV and Δφ=0.849 eV. The field raises the current by a factor eΔφ/kT=238 over plain Richardson emission (2.96×104 to 7.02×106 A/m2). The full integral gives 8.14×106 A/m2, 16 % above the Schottky formula; the excess is tunnelling through the top of the lowered barrier.

2.6.1One formula, three regimes

Dolan and Dyke (1954) did the integral of the master formula numerically, for a wide range of temperature, field and work function, and showed that it contains both the Fowler–Nordheim equation (cold, strong field) and the Richardson formula (hot, weak field). Our code does the same calculation (check C11: against the analytic Fowler–Nordheim formula the full integral is within 2.4 % at 4 and 5 V/nm; against Richardson–Schottky at 2800 K and 0.1 V/nm it is within 0.5 %). The regime is read from where the peak of the emitted electrons' energy distribution lies (section 2.7): below the Fermi level the source is a cold field emitter; between the Fermi level and the top of the barrier it is in the thermal-field regime; at the top, thermionic or Schottky.

2.7How wide is the energy: the spread ΔE

Lenses bend electrons of different energies by different amounts. The energy spread of the source therefore sets a blur in the probe (chapter 5), and it is the first of the four numbers we hand over.

Take electrons of total energy ε=w+εt​ leaving the surface. For each total energy, any normal energy w≤ε is allowed (the transverse part ε−w cannot be negative). Using F(w+εt​)=F(ε) in the integral (2.14) and changing variables from εt​ to ε,

P(ε)=F(ε)∫−∞ε​D(w)dw,J=eh34πm​∫P(ε)dε(2.26)

(the second relation, which the code checks, follows from integrating (2.14) by parts; check C12: ratio of the two currents 1+2.3e−05). With the linearised barrier, D∝ew/d, the inner integral is deε/d times constants and

P(ε)∝1+eε/kTeε/d​(2.27)

In words: the electrons that leave have energies spread from below the Fermi level (rising as eε/d: lower-lying electrons see a thicker barrier) to a cut-off at the Fermi level, smeared by kT. The peak is at ε∗=kTln[kT/(d−kT)], which exists when d>kT and lies below the Fermi level when d>2kT; the full integral puts it at −0.046 eV at the working point, just below the Fermi level. The full width at half maximum ΔE follows from the two roots of P=21​Pmax​: with d=0.175 eV and kT=0.0259 eV it is 0.218 eV from (2.27) and 0.215 eV from the full integral (check C13).

Because d∝F/φ​, the width grows with the field: ΔE=0.184, 0.215 and 0.245 eV at 3, 4 and 5 V/nm. A cold source gains in current by running at higher field and pays in energy width. For the Schottky preset the full integral gives ΔE=0.43 eV: the distribution is broad because it is a thermal tail above the barrier top, and its peak lies 0.15 eV above the top.

Against published values. A public Hitachi High-Tech page (8 May 2026), written for buyers of electron microscopes, quotes "around 0.2–0.3 eV" for cold field emission and "around 0.6–1.1 eV" for Schottky sources. Our cold value, 0.21 eV, lies in the first range and was not fitted to it. Our Schottky value, 0.43 eV, lies below the second range. The model contains no electron–electron interaction in the beam and no distribution of fields over the emitting area. Both widen the measured distribution (inference, not tested here); the vendor page is a marketing source and gives no conditions, so we use it only to show that the model is in the right range for the cold source and incomplete for the Schottky one.

2.8Brightness and the virtual source

A tip that emits a large current into a huge angle is useless for a probe, because only the electrons that go through a small aperture count. The quantity that matters is the current per unit area and per unit solid angle, the brightness.

The brightness B of a source is the current dI that comes from the area dA into the solid angle dΩ: B=dI/(dAdΩ). Chapter 3 shows (Liouville) that B/V does not change as the beam is accelerated through V (non-relativistically), so we give the reduced brightness Br​=B/V, in A m−2 sr−1 V−1.

2.8.1From the energy of the sideways motion to the angle

An electron with transverse energy εt​ that has been accelerated to the energy eV moves at a small angle α to the axis with α2≈εt​/(eV) (ratio of the transverse to the total kinetic energy). Electrons with transverse energy between εt​ and εt​+dεt​ therefore fill the solid angle dΩ=πd(α2)=πdεt​/(eV). Counting those electrons as in (2.14) but without integrating over εt​ gives the current density per unit transverse energy,

j(εt​)=eh34πm​∫D(w)F(w+εt​)dw(2.28)

so B=jπeV​ at εt​→0, where the direction is along the axis, and

Br​=πe​j(εt​=0)(2.29)

with j per joule, so ej is per electronvolt. For the cold limit, F is a step and j(εt​)=(J/d)e−εt​/d (integrate e−GF​ew/d up to w=−εt​ and compare with (2.19)). The mean transverse energy is then d, and

Br​=πdJ​(d in eV)(2.30)

At 4 V/nm this gives 2.11×108, the full integral 2.17×108 Am−2sr−1V−1 (check C14). The model's mean transverse energy is 0.168 eV (cold) and 0.155 eV (Schottky preset). The reduced brightness of the Schottky preset is 1.67×107, a factor 13 below the cold preset: the cold source wins by its current density, 1.16×108 against 8.14×106 A/m2, at similar transverse energy.

These are numbers for the emitting patch itself. A published reduced brightness of an operating source also includes everything between the patch and the measurement, and is dealt with in chapter 3, where we put published values next to ours. The vendor page of section 2.7 gives a brightness "up to about 109 A/cm²·sr" for cold field emission and "high, but generally lower" for Schottky, with no voltage; it is not a reduced brightness and we do not compare it with ours.

2.8.2The virtual source

The electrons do not all seem to come from the same point. Follow the backward extension of the straight path each electron has far away: these lines pass through a small disc, the virtual source, which is the object the lenses image. A first estimate comes from conservation of angular momentum. In a field that points along the radius from the apex centre, an electron leaving the sphere of radius r with transverse momentum pt​=2mεt​​ keeps L=pt​r for ever. Far away its momentum is p∞​=2meV​ and the extended path passes the centre at the distance

b=p∞​L​=reVεt​​​(2.31)

(check C17: a Runge–Kutta integration of the trajectory in a 1/r potential, to 2 mm, finds 0.70687 nm against 0.70686 nm). We define the virtual source diameter as dv​=2r⟨εt​⟩/(eV)​, with the mean transverse energy of the model. For the cold preset (r=50 nm, V=1000 V) it is 1.30 nm; for the Schottky preset (r=500 nm, V=2000 V) it is 8.8 nm. The Hitachi page quotes typical virtual source sizes of 2.5 to 5 nm (cold) and 15 to 30 nm (Schottky). Ours are lower for both; the model has a perfectly radial field, no extractor lens and an emitting patch of zero size. All three would increase dv​ (inference). We treat dv​ as a lower bound.

2.9Checking the model against a published tungsten tip

A model that has not met a measurement is a story. Here it meets one: the current–voltage curve of a tungsten tip measured by Ayari, Vincent, Perisanu, Poncharal and Purcell in 2023, whose raw numbers are public.

The measurement (their section III). A ⟨111⟩ tungsten tip, electrochemically etched from a 125 µm wire, initial radius about 15 nm, heated several times for 30 s at 1700 K. Base pressure 3×10−10 Torr (4×10−8 Pa). The current was collected by a microchannel plate and phosphor screen, in the range from femtoampere to picoampere; the voltage was swept five times up and down between 1300 V and 1630 V in steps of 10 V. We use their sweep "run 4, down" (33 points; data in data/ch02/ayari2023_w111_iv.csv, licence CC BY 4.0, provenance in the README of that folder).

What we did. (i) A straight line through ln(I/V2) against 1/V gives slope −41339 V and intercept 4.578, which reproduces the authors' own fit (41 339 ± 73 V, 4.57 ± 0.05; check C19) and so confirms that we read the units of the file correctly (current in nanoampere). (ii) With φ=4.5 eV, which the authors also assume, (2.23) with s(f)=0.974 at the middle of the range gives ζ=651 nm. (iii) The full fit of I=AJ(V/ζ) to all 33 points, with the temperature factor and 300 K, gives ζ=657.5 nm, an emitting area A=781 nm2, and a root-mean-square deviation of lnI of 1.8 %, largest deviation 5.8 %. With k=5 the radius is r=ζ/k=132 nm. The authors' own analysis with the Murphy–Good model has 653 nm and 131 nm for the same sweep (their file paramIV4d.txt), so the two calculations agree.

2.9.1Where model and data differ

The data do not fix the work function. The fit quality is the same, rms 0.0185 in lnI, for any φ between 4.0 and 5.5 eV; only ζ changes, because the slope fixes the product φ3/2ζ. For φ=4.0, 4.5, 5.0 and 5.5 eV the fit gives ζ=788, 658, 560 and 484 nm, so the apex radius deduced from a slope inherits the full uncertainty of φ and of k. The authors of the data make this point more strongly in their title and abstract. The model is not wrong here; the measurement is not sensitive enough to test it for φ.

The residuals. The model describes the curve to within 1.8 % rms over a range in which the current changes by a factor 752. The deviations look irregular. The authors report that the current at a fixed voltage drifts by about 8 % per hour (their Fig. 4); in the data file the current at 1470 V in the ten sweeps in time order is 0.000161, 0.000154, 0.00016, 0.000158, 0.00015, 0.00015, 0.000134, 0.000126, 0.000145, 0.000135 nA. Our residuals are of the size of that drift and the noise they quote (1.8 % standard deviation about their line), so the model has no deviation to explain that the measurement does not already contain (inference).

The radius. The fit gives ζ=kr=658 nm, a tip of 132 nm radius if k=5, against 15 nm initially. The authors expect the radius to increase because of the repeated heating; the field-emission measurement alone cannot say. It does not contradict the model, but it shows what the model cannot do: it does not predict the geometry.

The scaled field. The fit places the data at f=0.142 to 0.176 (F=1.99 to 2.48 V/nm), at the lower edge of the range that Forbes and co-workers call physically reasonable for a tungsten tip, 0.15≤f≤0.45, and well above the "clearly unreasonable" limit 0.10 (Allaham et al. 2022, their Table 1). The classical tungsten data set of Dyke and Trolan (1953, emitter X89), which Forbes (2013) re-analysed, covers 0.20<f<0.34; our working point f=0.28 lies inside that range. We did not open the paper of Dyke and Trolan (only its abstract is public), so no number from it enters this chapter.

2.10Vacuum and contamination

The current of a cold tip depends on φ so steeply that a few foreign atoms on the apex change it. How fast they arrive, and whether they leave again, is decided by the pressure and the temperature.

2.10.1How many molecules arrive: Hertz–Knudsen

The residual gas at temperature Tg​ and pressure p has density n=p/kTg​ and Maxwell–Boltzmann velocities, f(v)=(mg​/2πkTg​)3/2e−mg​v2/2kTg​. The molecules that hit a surface of unit area per second are those moving towards it, weighted by their normal speed:

Φ=n∫vx​>0​vx​f(v)d3v=n2πmg​kTg​​​=2πmg​kTg​​p​(2.32)

(check C15 does the three integrals symbolically). This is the Hertz–Knudsen flux. For hydrogen (mg​=2.016 u) at 300 K and 10−9 Pa, Φ=1.07×1014 m−2s−1; for carbon monoxide (28 u) 2.87×1013 m−2s−1. A surface of tungsten carries about Ns​=1/a2 atoms per unit area; with the lattice constant a=0.3165 nm this is 9.98×1018 m−2, and we use Ns​=1019 m−2. Dividing, the time to deposit one monolayer if every molecule sticks is Ns​/Φ:

pressure p (Pa)one monolayer of H2one monolayer of CO
10⁻⁴1 s3 s
10⁻⁶93 s6 min
10⁻⁸2.6 h9.7 h
10⁻⁹25.9 h4.0 days
10⁻¹⁰10.8 days40.3 days

This is the sense of the vacuum requirement: at 10−4 Pa a clean surface is covered in about a second for hydrogen and a few seconds for carbon monoxide (the table above); at 10−9 Pa, which is the figure that Applied Materials gives for its columns (it states "well below 1×10−11 millibar", that is below 10−9 Pa, in its press release of 14 December 2022, a public claim we quote and do not test), it takes 25.9 h for hydrogen at unit sticking.

2.10.2The rate equation

Let θ be the fraction of the apex sites that carry an adsorbed atom. Molecules arrive at Φ, a fraction s of those that hit a free site stick, and an adsorbed atom leaves at the rate kd​ per second. We allow a factor κ≥1 for gas that is collected on the shank and diffuses to the apex (κ=1 in the default). Then

dtdθ​=a(1−θ)−kd​θ,a=κsNs​Φ​,kd​=ν0​e−Ed​/kT(2.33)

This is first-order Langmuir kinetics: no interaction between adatoms, no precursor state, one adsorbate per site. The desorption rate has the Arrhenius form with an attempt frequency ν0​=1013 s−1 and a desorption energy Ed​; both are assumptions, discussed below. The equation has the solution (check C16, SymPy)

θ(t)=θ∞​+(θ0​−θ∞​)e−(a+kd​)t,θ∞​=a+kd​a​(2.34)

and the time to reach a coverage θ∗<θ∞​ from a clean surface is t∗=−ln(1−θ∗/θ∞​)/(a+kd​). When kd​ is negligible, t∗≈θ∗Ns​/(κsΦ) and, because Φ∝p, pt∗ is a constant. This is the prediction we test.

2.10.3Emission as a function of coverage (a model assumption)

Model assumption

We assume that the emitting surface is a patchwork: the fraction 1−θ with the clean work function φ, the fraction θ with φ+Δφads​. The current is the sum of the two contributions, I/I0​=(1−θ)+θρ with ρ=J(φ+Δφads​)/J(φ) at the same field. This is a choice made for simplicity; nothing in the derivation forces it. We take Δφads​=1.0 eV, which gives ρ=0.0021 at the working point; it is not a measured value. What is measured (Cho 2014, below) is that adsorption of residual gas, mostly hydrogen, lowers the current and that this is attributed to an increase of the work function.

How strongly the current reacts to the work function is a result of the Fowler–Nordheim equation, not of this assumption. The logarithmic derivatives at the working point are ∂lnJ/∂lnF=17.5 and ∂lnJ/∂lnφ=−26.6. A rise of φ by 0.1 eV (2.2 %) cuts the current density by the factor 0.55; a rise by 1 eV cuts it by 0.0021. A field higher by 10 % raises it by 4.9.

2.10.4The rate equation against a measurement

Cho (2014) measured the probe current of a W(310) tip in an extreme-high-vacuum chamber, after flash heating, while the pressure was changed with a getter pump. The residual gas was more than 99 % hydrogen (his Fig. 5). The probe current stays near its initial value for a time τ90​, until it has dropped by 10 %, and then falls quickly. He reports τ90​=15, 105 and 450 min at 2×10−8, 2–3×10−9 and 6–8×10−10 Pa (gauge readings; we take 2.5 and 7×10−10 Pa), and that the damping rate is proportional to the pressure. The products pτ90​ are 3.00×10−7, 2.63×10−7 and 3.15×10−7 Pa·min: constant within ±9 % over a factor 29 in pressure, as (2.33) with the Hertz–Knudsen flux says. Taking θ∗=0.1 for the 10 % drop (patch model with ρ≈0) and mg​=2.016 u, the product κs that each point needs is 0.52, 0.59 and 0.49, mean 0.54. This mean is what we use as the default of the simulation. The shape of the curve is a different matter: Cho's current stays flat and then falls quickly, while our patch model falls from the start, linearly in θ. The model reproduces the 1/p scaling of the time to a 10 % drop, not the shape of the decay; a model with a threshold (a site that matters only once its neighbours are covered) would be needed for that.

What this does and does not show. The data confirm the scaling τ∝1/p over one and a half decades. The size of the constant fixes one number, κs≈0.5, and so does not test the model independently: any combination of sticking, dissociation of H2 into two atoms, and θ∗ that multiplies to the same product fits. Cho notes also that the "stable region" is specific to the (310) plane and disappears when gases other than hydrogen are present; the model has no plane dependence and no species dependence beyond the flux. His own constant CCH​=1.93×10−7 Pa·min refers to a 50 % drop of the total emission current and is a different quantity.

2.10.5The flash-cleaning cycle

At room temperature kd​ is negligible: for Ed​=1.9 eV, kd​=1.2×10−19 s−1, so adsorbed atoms stay as long as the experiment lasts. This is why a cold tip cannot clean itself. Heating the tip for a few seconds changes the rate by many orders of magnitude: at 700 K, kd​=0.21 s−1; at 1000 K, 2657 s−1; at 2000 K, 1.6×108 s−1. A flash of 5 s at 1000 K therefore removes everything (e−kd​t≈0). The values Ed​=1.9 eV and ν0​=1013 s−1 are assumptions, chosen so that hydrogen-like adsorbates leave a hot tip within seconds near 700 K (a residence time 1/kd​=4.8 s there) and stay at room temperature; they are not measured for this tip. The cycle is then: run until I/I0​ falls below a threshold, flash, run again. With the threshold 0.7 the model flashes after 104 min at 10−8 Pa and hydrogen, and for the other pressures (same assumptions) after:

pressure (Pa)time between flashes
10⁻⁷10 min
10⁻⁸104 min
10⁻⁹17.3 h
10⁻¹⁰7.2 days
10⁻¹¹72.2 days

One atom. Applied Materials states publicly that "a single atom" on the tip can partly block the emission. In our patch model an adsorbed atom blocks only its own site, which at our working point is one of 8201 sites in the effective emitting area of 820 nm2 (current divided by current density), so a single atom changes the current by 1.2×10−4. The model does not reproduce the claim for a tip of this size. It does for a tip whose emission is concentrated on a few atoms, where one atom is a large fraction of the emitting area, and when an adsorbate changes φ over a region larger than its own footprint. The model has neither; this is a limit of the model that we do not hide (see section section 2.13).

2.11Why the cold tip is bright but fragile

The two properties come from the same exponent, and it is easier to see them together.

The tip is bright because of two concentrations. The field concentrates: F=V/(kr) turns a kilovolt into 4 V/nm. And the current concentrates: J varies as F17.5 locally, so electrons come out of a tiny patch (our effective emitting area is 820 nm², 5 % of the hemisphere, 15708 nm2) with a small transverse energy (0.17 eV). Brightness is current density over transverse energy (section 2.8), so a large current density at a small transverse energy is a high brightness. The tiny emitting area does not raise the brightness; it makes the virtual source small, which is what lets a column shrink it to a nanometre spot without throwing current away.

The tip is fragile because of the same exponent seen from the other side. The current depends on the work function with the logarithmic derivative −27: one adsorbed atom that raises the local work function by 0.1 eV removes 45 % of the current from where it sits, and by 1 eV removes 99.8 %. At 10−9 Pa a surface of tungsten receives a monolayer of hydrogen in 25.9 h (all molecules sticking) and the current falls by 10 % in a few hours. A Schottky emitter is hot, the adsorbates leave as fast as they come, and the current is steady; it pays with a lower brightness and a larger energy spread. A cold emitter has to be flashed.

The apex is drawn as a sphere on a cone; the model uses the cosine law F(ϑ)=F0​cosϑ of a sphere in a uniform field for the variation of the field over the cap, and integrates J over the cap of the hemisphere. 2.13Hand-over, limits and checks

2.13.1What chapter 3 receives

The four numbers handed to chapter 3, for the two presets, are computed by handover() in physics/ch02.js and ref/ch02.py (the two agree to a relative difference of 10−9; checks/check_parity.py). The simulation changes them when you move a slider or when time passes.

2.13.2What the model leaves out

Free-electron metal, no band structure and no crystal face dependence. A planar barrier with a classical image charge, and the WKB transmission without its prefactor. A hemispherical cap with F∝cosϑ, and k as a free number; no field solver (a proper one is outside this project). No Coulomb interaction between electrons, hence no Boersch effect and no space-charge limit on the brightness. A radial-field estimate of the virtual source. Contamination as one species, first-order kinetics, no surface diffusion, with Ed​, ν0​, κ and Δφads​ assumed, and s obtained from one data set. No tip blunting by the high-temperature flash, no ion bombardment of the tip, no emission-pattern change. Each omission is a place where a real column's source module differs; none is a claim about any particular product.

Problems

1. A tip of radius 30 nm with k=5 is operated at 800 V. Find F, f, v (Forbes) and J0​ for φ=4.5 eV. Answer: F=5.33 V/nm, f=0.379, v=0.559, J0​=9.23×109 A/m2.

2. Show from G=bφ3/2v(f)/F that ∂lnJ/∂lnφ≈−23​bφ3/2t(f)/F when the prefactor is neglected, and evaluate it at the working point. Answer: −23​×16.30×1.051=−25.7; the complete derivative, with the prefactor, is −26.6.

3. With s=1, how long does a clean tungsten surface take to receive one monolayer of CO at 10−7 Pa, and of H2? Answer: 3479 s and 933 s.

Chapter 3Acceleration, brightness, energy spread

The gun turns a voltage into kinetic energy; relativity turns that energy into a momentum and a wavelength; Liouville’s theorem says the column can never make the source brighter. This chapter derives the beam voltage V∗, the angle change when the beam is slowed before the wafer, the conservation of reduced brightness, and the probe current that a given brightness allows, and puts the source of chapter 2 next to published values.

3.1The gun: a step in potential

A marble let go at the top of a smooth slide arrives at the bottom with a speed that depends only on how far it has dropped, not on the shape of the slide. An electron in a static electric field is that marble. In §1.5 we found that in static fields the energy γmc2+qφ is conserved, with q=−e the electron's charge and φ the electric potential. An electron that leaves the tip at rest (on the scale of what follows) and arrives where the potential is higher by V has therefore gained the kinetic energy

E0​=(γ−1)mc2=eV,γ=1+mc2eV​.
(3.1)

Nothing else about the path enters. This is why an electron gun can be built from simple parts: the tip of §2.1, an extractor a fraction of a millimetre away whose voltage Vex​ pulls the electrons out by tunnelling, and an anode whose voltage Vacc​ sets their final energy. The two knobs do different jobs. Vex​, together with the tip radius, fixes the field at the apex and therefore the current and its energy spread (chapter 2). Vacc​ fixes the energy with which the electrons travel down the column, and with it their wavelength, how stiffly they resist the lenses, and how deep they would go into the wafer. Figure 3.1 shows the potential energy U=−eφ of an electron along the axis: a drop of eVacc​ in the gun, a flat floor in the column, and, if the wafer is held at a less positive potential, a step back up to −eVland​ just before the wafer.

One correction to "at rest". Electrons leave a cold tip with energies within a few tenths of an electronvolt of the Fermi level (chapter 2 found a width of 0.215 eV at the working point). Measured from the Fermi level, every electron then gains exactly eV; the spread is carried along unchanged. We come back to this in §3.6.

3.2Momentum and wavelength, exactly

The wavelength that decides how small a spot can be (chapter 5) is the de Broglie wavelength λ=h/p, so we need the momentum p that belongs to the kinetic energy eV. For a particle of rest energy mc2, total energy E and momentum p, special relativity gives E2=(pc)2+(mc2)2. With E=mc2+eV from (3.1),

(pc)2=(mc2+eV)2−(mc2)2=(eV)2+2eVmc2.

We divide by c2 and take 2meV out as a factor:

p2=2meV(1+2mc2eV​)≡2meV∗,V∗=V(1+2mc2eV​).
(3.2)

The quantity V∗ is the relativistically corrected voltage. Its use is that every non-relativistic formula of electron optics in which V stands for p2/(2me) becomes exact when V is replaced by V∗. The wavelength is then

λ=ph​=2meV∗​h​.
(3.3)
Key result · the beam voltage

After a potential step V the electron has p2=2meV∗ with V∗=V(1+eV/2mc2), and λ=h/2meV∗​. In every formula below, the beam voltage means V∗.

Two limits check (3.3). When eV≪mc2= 510.999 keV, the bracket is 1 and λ→h/2meV​, the school formula. When eV≫mc2, the term (eV)2 dominates, p→eV/c and λ→hc/(eV), the wavelength of a photon of the same energy: the electron's rest mass no longer matters. Both limits are verified symbolically (check D2 in §3.8).

How large is the correction? The non-relativistic formula overestimates the wavelength by the factor V∗/V​=1+eV/2mc2​≈1+eV/(4mc2) (check D3), which passes one per cent at 20.5 kV.

Example 3.1 · wavelengths along the range of electron microscopes

At 1 kV, V∗= 1000.98 V and λ= 38.76 pm; the non-relativistic formula is off by 0.049 %. At V= 30000 V, V∗/V= 1.02935, γ= 1.05871 and λ= 6.979 pm, an error of 1.5 % without relativity. At 100 kV, λ= 3.701 pm (error 4.8 %), and at V= 3.00 × 10⁵ V, λ= 1.969 pm, where the photon-like limit hc/eV would give 4.13 pm: at 300 kV neither limit will do. The exact wavelength is shorter than both, because p2c2=(eV)2+2eVmc2 is larger than each of its two terms. A low-voltage scanning microscope, which works at a few hundred volts to a few kilovolts, can use the school formula to a fraction of a per cent; a transmission microscope cannot.

3.3Landing softly: deceleration before the wafer

The energy that is best for the column is often not the energy that is best for the wafer. A fast beam is stiff: it is less disturbed by stray fields and by the repulsion between its own electrons, and the lens aberrations that grow with the relative energy spread ΔE/E (chapter 5) are smaller. A slow beam is gentle: it deposits its energy in the top few nanometres, charges insulators less and damages fragile resist less (chapter 6). A column can have both by running at Vacc​ and slowing the electrons in a retarding field between the last lens and the wafer, which is held at a potential Vacc​−Vland​ below the column, so that the electrons land with eVland​ (Figure 3.1).

What happens to the beam's angles? Near the axis of a round system the retarding field points along the axis. It changes the axial momentum pz​ and leaves the transverse momentum p⊥​ alone, as a ball thrown sideways while it rolls up a ramp keeps its sideways push. The angle of a ray to the axis is tanα=p⊥​/pz​, and for small angles pz​≈p, so

ααland​​=pland​pacc​​=Vland∗​Vacc∗​​​.
(3.4)

(check D4). A beam slowed down opens up. This is not a loss: as §3.4 shows, the brightness per volt is unchanged, so a spot that is smaller in angle at the column energy is simply larger in angle at the wafer, and the current is the same.

Example 3.2 · a column at 5 kV landing at 800 V

The angle grows by (3.4): αland​/α= 2.51. The wavelength grows from 17.3 pm in the column to 43.3 pm at the wafer, by the same factor as the angle, so the diffraction blur λ/α is unchanged. What deceleration buys is elsewhere: the beam crosses the column and its lenses at the higher energy, where the relative energy spread ΔE/E (and with it the chromatic blur, chapter 5) is smaller and the electrons push each other less, and it still lands gently. The simulation's default (1 kV landing at 800 V) gives a factor 1.118.

The model is the paraxial one: a uniform retarding field along the axis and no fringe fields at its edges. This hides a large effect. Where the field begins and ends it bends the rays (an aperture lens), and for a gap of a millimetre or so its focal length is of the order of a working distance, so it is not a small correction: in a real column the retarding field and the objective are designed together as one immersion lens. Chapter 4 models the magnetic objective alone, and this overlap is outside the project.

3.4Brightness, and why the column cannot raise it

A lens can make a spot smaller only by making its angles larger, as a magnifying glass that concentrates sunlight into a small dot does so by bringing the light in from a wide cone. The quantity that no lens can change is the current per area per solid angle, the brightness,

B=dAdΩdI​,
(3.5)

in A m−2 sr−1. The reason is Liouville's theorem; the next two paragraphs (★) prove it, and the result is restated after them. Take the distance z along the axis as the "time" and follow the electrons that cross a plane z at transverse position x with transverse momentum px​. In a static field the energy is fixed, and the motion from plane to plane is generated by the Hamiltonian

H(x,px​;z)=−pz​=−P(x,z)2−(px​−qAx​)2​,

where px​ is the canonical momentum (chapter 1), P(x,z) the total momentum the potential allows at that point and Ax​ the vector potential; a round magnetic lens has no Az​ near the axis. Hamilton's equations, dx/dz=∂H/∂px​ and dpx​/dz=−∂H/∂x, define a flow in the plane (x,px​) whose divergence is

∂x∂​∂px​∂H​−∂px​∂​∂x∂H​=0,

because mixed derivatives commute (check D5, done symbolically for one transverse dimension). With two transverse dimensions a magnetic lens couples x and y (it rotates the beam), but the motion is still generated by a Hamiltonian H(x,y,px​,py​;z), and the divergence of its flow in four dimensions is a sum of the same commuting mixed derivatives, again zero: Liouville's theorem. A flow with no divergence carries a patch of phase space without changing its area, as an incompressible fluid carries a drop of ink: the patch can be stretched into a long thin streak (a focus) but not shrunk (Figure 3.2). In two transverse dimensions the conserved quantity is dAd2p⊥​.

The solid angle of a narrow cone of directions is dΩ=d2p⊥​/p2, since a direction differs from the axis by p⊥​/p in each transverse coordinate. So dAdΩp2 is conserved, and with it B/p2. With p2=2meV∗ from (3.2) the conserved quantity is the reduced brightness

Br​=V∗B​.
(3.6)
Key result · reduced brightness is conserved

Without collisions between the beam's electrons, Br​=B/V∗ has the same value at every plane of the column, whatever lenses, apertures (which remove current but do not raise Br​) and accelerating or retarding fields lie between (check D6, which follows from D5 and (3.2); it is exact in V∗ and holds to first order in the beam angle, through dΩ=d2p⊥​/p2). A column can at best keep the brightness its source gives; it can never raise it.

This is why chapter 2 spent so long on the tip. Every gain in probe current at a given spot size must come from the source.

3.5From brightness to probe current

Chapter 2 computed the brightness of the emitting patch on the axis, Br​=ej(εt​=0)/π, where j(εt​) is the emitted current density per unit transverse energy; for the exponential distribution of transverse energies of chapter 2 this equals eJ/(π⟨εt​⟩), the current from an infinitesimal area at the centre of the source into an infinitesimal solid angle. A probe, however, is an image of the whole virtual source. Each electron appears in the virtual-source plane at a distance proportional to its transverse velocity, and an exponential distribution of εt​∝vt2​ maps onto a Gaussian distribution of that distance (Bronsgeest et al. 2008, section VI): the virtual source is Gaussian, brightest at the centre. Bronsgeest, Barth, Swanson and Kruit (2008) define the practical brightness as the total angular current density divided by the area of the disk that holds half of the current (the "FW50" diameter d), and show that it fixes the probe current (their Eq. 6):

Ip​=Bpr​V∗4πd2​πα2,
(3.7)

with α the half-angle of the beam at the wafer and d the FW50 diameter of the source image there; πα2 is the small-angle solid angle of the cone (check D8).

The step from the axial value to the practical one is short. A Gaussian profile J(r)=J0​e−r2/σ2 carries the total current πσ2J0​; the current inside radius R is πσ2J0​(1−e−R2/σ2), which is half the total when R2=σ2ln2. The total divided by the area πR2 of that disk is J0​/ln2. Hence

Bpr​=ln2Br​​=1.4427Br​,
(3.8)

(check D7). Bronsgeest et al. write this as 1.44ej/(π⟨εt​⟩) (their Eqs. 15 and 16) and call the factor "a surprising, new result"; our derivation shows where it comes from. It does not contradict §3.4: nothing has been made brighter. The factor comes only from the definition, which divides the whole current by the area of the disk that holds half of it. It holds as long as the electrons do not push each other between the tip and the extractor.

Example 3.3 · the probe current of the cold tip

The cold tip of chapter 2 (clean, 4 V/nm) has Br​= 2.17 × 10⁸ A m−2 sr−1 V−1, so Bpr​= 3.13 × 10⁸ A m−2 sr−1 V−1. Land at 800 V (V∗= 800.63 V), form a source image of d= 1 nm with α= 5 mrad, and (3.7) gives Ip​= 15 pA, about 97 electrons per microsecond. The 1 nm is the size of the source image alone; the probe is larger, because diffraction at this angle adds a blur of FW50 diameter 0.66λ/α= 5.7 nm (Bronsgeest et al., Eq. 19), and chapter 5 adds the aberrations. The Schottky preset of chapter 2 would give 1.2 pA in the same spot: its practical brightness is lower by a factor 13. Chapter 7 shows that a few thousand electrons per pixel are needed for a clean edge, and this is where the trade-off of chapter 0 bites: half the spot diameter at the same angle means a quarter of the current.

3.6Energy spread through the column

Two electrons that leave the tip with energies Ea​ and Eb​ each gain eV in a static field, so their difference Ea​−Eb​ is unchanged (check D9). The energy spread ΔE of the source, 0.215 eV for the cold tip of chapter 2 and 0.43 eV for its Schottky preset, is carried to the wafer as it is. What changes is the relative spread ΔE/(eV): 2.1×10−4 at 1 kV, 2.7×10−4 at 800 V. Chapter 5 shows that the chromatic blur of the spot is proportional to this ratio, which is why low-voltage columns prize the narrow spread of the cold source.

The statement "unchanged" assumes that the electrons of the beam do not exchange energy with one another. Where the beam is dense, near the source and at crossovers, the random Coulomb pushes between electrons widen the distribution, the Boersch effect, and also blur the spot sideways. Both grow with the current and are the reason why practical brightness stops rising at high emission current. This project does not model them; the numbers here are lower bounds on the spread an operating gun shows.

3.7The model next to published source data

How do the brightness and energy spread of chapter 2 compare with what real guns achieve? Williams and Carter (Transmission Electron Microscopy, ch. 5, Table 5.1) list typical values, stated at 100 kV, digitised with their provenance in this project's data folder (data/ch02/source_properties_williams_carter.csv). The book does not say which brightness it lists (axial or practical) or which width its energy spread is; the model's spread is the full width at half maximum. They are round textbook numbers, good to a factor of about two, not measurements with uncertainties. We convert their brightness to reduced brightness with V∗ at 100 kV (1.09785 × 10⁵ V, a correction of 9.8 % over dividing by V).

sourcemodel Br​, axialmodel Bpr​Williams & Carter B/V∗model / bookmodel ΔE (eV)book ΔE (eV)
cold field emission2.17 × 10⁸3.13 × 10⁸9.11 × 10⁷2.4 to 3.40.2150.300
Schottky1.67 × 10⁷2.41 × 10⁷4.55 × 10⁷0.37 to 0.530.430.700

(Brightness in A m−2 sr−1 V−1; the last brightness column gives the ratio for the axial and the practical value.) The brightness agrees in order of magnitude for both sources and no better: the model is higher than the book by a factor 2.4 to 3.4 for the cold source, more than the factor of about two the table carries, and lower by a factor 0.37 to 0.53 for the Schottky preset. Neither gap is surprising. For the cold source the model is the intrinsic brightness of a clean patch, which an operating gun cannot keep once the electrons interact; for the Schottky preset the work function and apex field are assumptions of chapter 2, and the current density depends on them exponentially. The energy spreads of the model are smaller than the book's, by about a third for both. That is the direction we expect: the model is the intrinsic emission of a clean surface, while the book's values belong to operating guns, which add the Boersch broadening of §3.6. For the Schottky preset the model also assumes a work function and an apex field that chapter 2 states as assumptions. Bronsgeest et al. note, for Schottky sources, that the interactions become important above a practical brightness of about 3×108 A m−2 sr−1 V−1; our Schottky preset sits at 0.080 of that, so the model's neglect of interactions is consistent for it. They give no such mark for cold emitters; if the same order holds there, the cold source at 3.13 × 10⁸ is near it, and its predicted brightness is best read as an upper limit for an operating gun.

The browser module physics/ch03.js and the Python reference ref/ch03.py evaluate the same closed formulas; they agree to the last bits of a 64-bit number (the parity check states a tolerance of 10−14). Every number in this chapter's text is produced by one of them or by chapter 2's module, and checked against the other, except three kinds: constants computed in text/ch03.py from CODATA 2018 (mc2, h/2me​, 1/ln2), values quoted from Williams and Carter and from Bronsgeest et al., named as such, and the givens of the examples.

What chapter 4 and chapter 5 receive. The column voltage Vacc∗​, the landing voltage Vland∗​ and the wavelength there, the angle factor (3.4), and the rule (3.7) with Bpr​=Br​/ln2 for the probe current.

What the model leaves out. Electron–electron interactions (Boersch broadening, trajectory displacement, space charge); the gun's own lens action and aberrations, which matter at large emission angles; the overlap of the retarding field with the objective lens; any noise or ripple of the high-voltage supply, which adds to ΔE directly. The next, more complete model would trace electrons through a computed gun field with their mutual forces (a Monte Carlo of Coulomb interactions), which is how the practical brightness of a real gun is predicted.

Chapter 4The lens

A short coil in an iron shell focuses electrons as a glass lens focuses light, because the field lines that bulge out of its gap first twist the electron about the axis and then push it inwards, in proportion to its distance from the axis. We derive the field near the axis from Maxwell’s equations, the twist from Busch’s theorem and the paraxial ray equation from the radial force; solve Glaser’s bell-shaped lens exactly; focus it on the wafer; and measure its spherical and chromatic aberration by tracing rays, checked against the aberration integrals.

4.1From the helix to a lens

In §1.7 an electron in a long uniform magnetic field ran on a helix and came back to the axis after one turn, wherever it had started from on the axis and at whatever small angle: a uniform field images a point onto a point. A long solenoid is an awkward lens, because the image lies a whole turn away and the field fills all the space between. Shorten the field to a few millimetres, as a coil wound inside an iron shell with a narrow gap does (Figure 4.1), and the electron gets only a short kick on its way through. The kick is towards the axis and grows in proportion to the distance from it. That is exactly what a convex glass lens does to light, and it is why a short coil focuses.

The puzzle is how a magnetic field can push an electron towards the axis at all. On the axis the field points along the axis, and an electron moving along the axis feels nothing (v×B=0). Off the axis the field lines are not parallel to the axis near the gap: on the way into the gap they converge towards it, and on the way out they spread again, so the field has a radial part Br​. An electron moving along z through Br​ gets a force −evz​Br​ in the azimuthal direction: it starts to turn about the axis. Once it turns, its azimuthal velocity vθ​ crosses the axial field Bz​, and −evθ​Bz​ points towards the axis. The twist comes first, and the twist turned by the axial field is the focusing push. The next three sections make this exact.

4.2The field near the axis

Between the pole pieces there are no currents and the field is static, so ∇⋅B=0 and ∇×B=0. For a round lens nothing depends on the angle θ about the axis, and the field has a radial part Br​(r,z) and an axial part Bz​(r,z). In cylindrical coordinates the two equations are

r1​∂r∂(rBr​)​+∂z∂Bz​​=0,∂z∂Br​​−∂r∂Bz​​=0.
(4.1)

Near the axis we expand in powers of r. By symmetry Bz​ is even in r and Br​ is odd: Bz​=B(z)+b2​(z)r2+… and Br​=c1​(z)r+c3​(z)r3+…, where B(z) is the field on the axis, the one function a lens designer measures or computes. The first equation of (4.1) at order r0 gives 2c1​+B′=0, so c1​=−B′/2. The second at order r1 gives c1′​−2b2​=0, so b2​=−B′′/4. One more order of each gives c3​=B′′′/16. Hence

Bz​=B(z)−4r2​B′′(z)+…,Br​=−2r​B′(z)+16r3​B′′′(z)+…
(4.2)

(check L2 verifies that these satisfy both equations up to the next order). The whole field near the axis is fixed by B(z) and its derivatives. The radial part is the bending of the field lines: by (4.2) it points inwards where B rises along z (the lines converge into the gap) and outwards where B falls.

For B(z) we take Glaser's bell-shaped field (W. Glaser, Z. Physik 117, 285, 1941),

B(z)=1+(z/a)2B0​​,
(4.3)

with its peak B0​ at the centre of the gap and half-width a at half maximum. It is a fair description of a real pole-piece lens and has the rare virtue that its rays can be found exactly (§4.4). The peak follows from Ampère's law. Take a loop that runs along the axis from −∞ to +∞ and closes far away, outside the iron, where the field vanishes. The whole loop is in vacuum, where B=μ0​H, and it links the current of the N turns once, so ∮H⋅dl=NI gives ∫Bdz=μ0​NI exactly, whatever the iron does: the iron shapes B(z), it does not change its integral. With (4.3) the integral along the axis is πaB0​ (check L1), so

B0​=πaμ0​NI​.
(4.4)

What the iron decides is how concentrated the field is: a narrow gap gives a small a and, for the same NI, a high peak. That works only while the pole tips are not saturated; iron saturates at about 2 T, and a lens pushed towards that loses the bell shape that (4.3) assumes.

4.3Busch’s theorem and the paraxial ray equation

The twist of §4.1 follows from a conservation law. In chapter 1 the Lagrangian L=−mc2/γ−qφ+qv⋅A gave the canonical momentum p=γmv+qA (§1.4). A round lens has no preferred angle, so L does not depend on θ and the angular component of canonical momentum is conserved:

pθ​=γmr2θ˙+qrAθ​=const.
(4.5)

Near the axis the vector potential of a field B(z) is azimuthal, and Stokes' theorem on a circle of radius r gives 2πrAθ​=πr2B, the flux through the circle; so Aθ​=rB/2. Electrons that leave a point on the axis, as in a probe column, start with pθ​=0 (they have r=0), so with q=−e

θ˙=2γmeB(z)​
(4.6)

(check L4). This is Busch's theorem (H. Busch, Annalen der Physik 386, 974, 1926, doi 10.1002/andp.19263862507; we found its record, not its text): the electron turns about the axis at the Larmor rate, half the cyclotron rate, wherever the field is, and stops turning when it leaves the field. The image is therefore rotated, by θrot​=∫θ˙dt=2pe​∫Bdz along the path.

Now the radial motion. The radial component of the magnetic force qv×B is q(vθ​Bz​−vz​Bθ​)=qrθ˙B near the axis, since Bθ​=0 for a round lens and Bz​≈B. The radial equation of motion in cylindrical coordinates, with γ constant in a magnetic field, is

γm(r¨−rθ˙2)=qrθ˙B=−erθ˙B.

Insert (4.6): the right side is −e2B2r/(2γm), and the centrifugal term γmrθ˙2 is e2B2r/(4γm). Their sum gives

r¨=−(2γmeB​)2r.

The force is towards the axis and proportional to r: the lens law. Half of the magnetic push is used up keeping the electron on its turning path; the other half focuses. For paraxial rays z˙≈v, so d/dt=vd/dz, and with p=γmv and p2=2meV∗ from chapter 3,

r′′(z)=−4p2e2B2​r=−ηB(z)2r,η=8mV∗e​
(4.7)

(check L5). So far the ray started on the axis: it turns about the axis with the Larmor rate and its distance r from the axis obeys (4.7). A ray that starts off the axis with a sideways velocity (a skew ray) has pθ​=0, and the argument must be redone. Write the transverse position as one complex number w=x+iy. With Bx​=−xB′/2, By​=−yB′/2 from (4.2) the transverse force, written as one complex number, is

q[(v×B)x​+i(v×B)y​]=−iq[Bw˙+21​vB′w],

so with q=−e and d/dt=vd/dz

w′′=iκ(2Bw′+B′w),κ=2pe​.

Now look at the ray from a frame that turns about the axis by the angle θ(z) with θ′=κB: put w=ueiθ. The terms in u′ and B′ cancel, and what remains is u′′=−κ2B2u, with κ2=e/(8mV∗)=η (check L8). Both components of u obey (4.7), for every paraxial ray, skew or not. In the turning frame the lens acts as a plain radial focusing force; the turning itself is the image rotation.

The equation is linear: any sum of two solutions is a solution. Every ray from an object point at transverse position u0​ is u=u0​g(z)+αh(z), where g starts at height 1 with zero slope and h starts on the axis with unit slope. If the lens makes h return to the axis at some plane, every ray from that object point arrives there at the same place u0​g, whatever its angle α: a point is imaged onto a point. That linearity is what makes a sharp image possible at all.

Key result · the round magnetic lens

In the frame turning at the Larmor rate eB/(2γm), all paraxial rays obey r′′=−ηB2r with η=e/(8mV∗). The lens strength depends on B2/V∗: the same lens focuses a beam of four times the voltage at twice the current. The image is turned by θrot​=e/(8mV∗)​∫Bdz.

4.4Glaser’s exact solution★

With the bell field (4.3), (4.7) reads r′′+k2a2r/(a2+z2)2=0 with the dimensionless strength k2=ηB02​a2. Glaser's substitution z=acotψ maps the axis from z=−∞ to +∞ onto ψ from π to 0; together with the new unknown y=rsinψ it turns the equation into d2y/dψ2+ω2y=0 with ω2=1+k2, an oscillator with constant coefficients. Its solutions are sines of ωψ, and dividing by sinψ gives r. Its solution for a ray that arrives parallel to the axis at unit height is

r=ωsinψsin(ω(π−ψ))​,ω=1+k2​
(4.8)

(check L6 confirms the equation symbolically). Far before the lens, ψ→π and r→1. Far behind it, ψ→0 with z≈a/ψ, and expanding the sine gives r≈sin(ωπ)z/(ωa)−cos(ωπ): a straight line of slope sin(ωπ)/(ωa). A ray that came in parallel at unit height leaves with slope −1/f, so the focal length is

f=−sin(ωπ)ωa​.
(4.9)

For 1<ω<2 the sine is negative and f is positive: one crossing of the axis, a converging lens. For a weak lens, k→0, sin(ωπ)≈−πk2/2 and 1/f→πk2/(2a), which is the thin-lens formula 1/f=η∫B2dz (check L7): the lens strength is the integral of the square of the field. The square explains why a lens cannot tell north from south, and why designers concentrate the field in a short gap: the same NI spread over half the length gives twice the ∫B2.

4.5The objective lens, focused on the wafer

The last lens of a probe column, the objective, takes a small source image (or a crossover) far above it and forms a much smaller image on the wafer. Its operator focuses by turning the lens current. Our solver does the same: it places the object a distance u before the lens centre, the wafer a working distance WD behind it, starts a paraxial ray from the axis at the object, and adjusts B0​ by bisection until the ray crosses the axis exactly at the wafer. The integration runs in the variable τ with z=atanτ, so that the steps crowd into the lens; it is the classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta method with a fixed number of steps.

The magnification follows from the angles. Liouville's theorem of chapter 3 at one voltage says that the product of the image size and the beam angle is fixed (the Lagrange invariant), so M=αobject​/αimage​, read off the slopes of the same ray at both ends.

Example 4.1 · the default objective

A gap field of half-width a= 2 mm, the object 0.2 m before it, the wafer 3 mm behind its centre, electrons of 800 V. Focusing needs NI= 346 A, a peak field B0​= 69.2 mT (by (4.4), μ0​NI/(πa)= 69.2 mT), In the dimensionless strength k2=ηB02​a2 and ω=1+k2​ of §4.4 this is k2= 0.525, ω= 1.235. The focal length (4.9) is f= 3.669 mm, 1.83 times a. It describes the straight lines that rays follow far outside the field, the way focal and principal planes describe a thick glass lens. The wafer is not far outside: at 3 mm =1.5a the field is still 31 % of B0​, 21 mT, and the rays are still bending when they arrive, so the thin-lens equation with f and u would not give the wafer's position. That is why the solver focuses the actual ray on the wafer and reads M from its actual slopes. The lens demagnifies by 55.5 (M= 0.0180), so a source image of 50 nm becomes 0.90 nm. The image is turned by 1.84 rad, 106°.

Example 4.2 · the same lens at 30 kV

At 30 kV the lens must be excited with NI= 2150 A, a factor 6.211 more, which is V30kV∗​/V800V∗​​= 6.211: by (4.7) the optics depend only on B2/V∗, so a fixed geometry with B0​∝V∗​ has the same focal length, magnification and aberrations (Cs​= 4.19 mm against 4.19 mm). The rotation is unchanged too, 1.84 rad. The scaling holds for a real lens only while its iron is not saturated: this lens needs a peak of 0.43 T at 30 kV, well below the 2 T at which iron saturates, but a shorter, stronger lens at high voltage reaches that limit.

4.6Why a round lens is never perfect: spherical and chromatic aberration

Equation (4.7) is exact only for rays infinitely close to the axis. A real ray at angle α departs from it in two ways: it feels the r3 terms of the field (4.2), and its own motion is not paraxial (its speed along the axis is smaller than v by the part that goes sideways and round the axis, which adds terms in B4). Both are third order in the ray's height and slope, and in a magnetic lens they always focus the outer rays more strongly than the inner ones, as a glass ball does: rays through the rim cross the axis before the paraxial image. At the image plane they miss the axis by

Δrs​=Cs​α3,
(4.10)

the spherical aberration, with α the half-angle of the ray at the image and Cs​ a length. A ray of a slightly different energy, eV∗(1+δ), sees a lens of strength η/(1+δ) and focuses at a different place: it misses by Δrc​=Cc​αδ, the chromatic aberration. (Here Δr is the radius in the Gaussian image plane; chapter 5 turns these into disc diameters.)

Scherzer proved in 1936 (Z. Physik 101, 593) that Cs​ and Cc​ are always positive for a lens that is static, round, free of charge on the axis and forms a real image. No arrangement of coils and iron of that kind can cancel them; one has to break one of the assumptions, which is what multipole aberration correctors do. This project does not model correctors.

How we measure them. We trace rays without the paraxial approximation. The solver follows the exact equation of motion of an electron in a static magnetic field, with z as the variable and the speed constant, through the field (4.2) kept to third order in r; it launches rays from the axial object point at image angles of 2 and 4 mrad, measures how far each misses the axis at the paraxial image, removes the tiny linear part left by the discretisation (a ray of 10−9 rad at the object, traced on the same grid, gives it; its own cubic miss is then negligible), and solves Δr=Cs​α3+C5​α5 for Cs​. For Cc​ it runs the paraxial ray at V∗(1±10−4) and takes the central difference.

How we check them. ★ For Cc​ there is a short proof. Let h(z) be the paraxial ray from the axial object point at zo​, scaled to unit slope at the image plane zi​, so h(zi​)=0, h′(zi​)=1; the ray of image angle α is αh. An electron of energy eV∗(1+δ) sees η/(1+δ)≈η(1−δ), so its ray αh+Δ obeys, to first order in δ, Δ′′+ηB2Δ=δηB2αh. Take a second paraxial ray g that is independent of h; their Wronskian W=gh′−hg′ is constant along z because neither equation has a first-derivative term, and at the image it equals g(zi​). Variation of constants gives the miss at the image,

Δ(zi​)=∫zo​zi​​Wh(z)g(zi​)−g(z)h(zi​)​δηB2αhdz=δαη∫zo​zi​​B2h2dz.

So Cc​=η∫zo​zi​​B2h2dz, and the solver's central difference agrees with this integral to all printed digits: 2.84759 mm against 2.84759 mm (check N2). For Cs​ the standard aberration integral, over the same range from object to image, is (P. W. Hawkes and E. Kasper, Principles of Electron Optics, vol. 1, Academic Press 1989; we took the formula as it is quoted in the lens-design literature and did not open the book, so our check of it is the agreement below)

Cs​=128mV∗e​∫[mV∗3e​B4h4+8B′2h4−8B2h2h′2]dz.
(4.11)

Evaluated on a fine grid it gives 4.18897 mm; the traced value is 4.18897 mm (check N3). The two methods have nothing in common but the field, and they agree to about one part in ten million, so each checks the other. The traced miss grows as α3 to 0.02 % between 1 and 8 mrad (check N5), and the traced focal length equals Glaser's (4.9), 3.669080 against 3.669080 mm; they differ only in the eighth digit, because the solver starts its parallel ray at a finite distance (check N1).

Example 4.3 · what the aberrations cost

The default objective has Cs​= 4.19 mm and Cc​= 2.85 mm, of the order of the focal length, as for most real objectives. For a beam of 5 mrad half-angle the spherical miss is Cs​α3= 0.52 nm, and with the 0.215 eV spread of chapter 2 at 800 V the chromatic miss is Cc​αΔE/E= 3.8 nm: at 800 V the chromatic aberration is the larger of the two, which is why low-voltage columns care so much about the energy spread of their source. Diffraction is larger still at this angle: the radius of the Airy disc, 0.61λ/α, is 5.3 nm. Moving the wafer to 5 mm raises them to 12.9 and 4.65 mm (f= 5.30 mm); a sharper field of a= 1 mm with the wafer 2 mm from the centre lowers them to 3.79 and 1.84 mm and needs 295 A. Short working distance and a short, strong field are what make a good objective; chapter 5 shows how the beam angle is then chosen to balance diffraction against these blurs.

4.7Electric lenses, briefly

An electric field can focus too. The same expansion as in §4.2, applied to Laplace's equation for the potential, gives near the axis φ(r,z)=ϕ(z)−4r2​ϕ′′(z)+…, with ϕ(z) the potential on the axis. The radial field Er​=−∂φ/∂r=2r​ϕ′′ again grows in proportion to r, so a region where ϕ′′=0 acts as a lens, converging or diverging depending on the sign and on how the electron's speed changes on the way. The retarding field of chapter 3 is such a lens. Electric lenses are common in the gun and in low-voltage columns, where the retarding field and the objective overlap; their paraxial equation contains ϕ′ and ϕ′′ besides ϕ and is solved in the same way. This project models only the magnetic objective, and it has no field solver: both lens fields are analytic models, and a real design starts from a computed field (finite or boundary elements) of the actual pole pieces and electrodes.

The browser module physics/ch04.js and the Python reference ref/ch04.py run the same Runge–Kutta integrals on the same grid of 6000 steps, 60 bisection steps for the focus; they agree to about 10−11 in every output (parity check).

What chapter 5 receives. Cs​ and Cc​ referred to the image (the wafer). The magnification M from the object to the wafer is reported but not handed on: in chapter 5 the size of the source image on the wafer follows from the source brightness and the asked current. The lens here is computed at the landing voltage, that is, without a retarding field; in a column that decelerates the beam in front of the wafer, as in chapter 3's 5 kV to 800 V case, the electrons pass the objective at the higher voltage, and the overlapping electric and magnetic fields would have to be solved together.

What the model leaves out. The field is an analytic bell, not the computed field of real pole pieces; iron losses and saturation; misalignment of the lens with the beam and the off-axis aberrations (coma, astigmatism, field curvature, distortion) that it causes; the overlap with a retarding field; condenser lenses, whose aberrations the objective demagnifies. Each is a known part of real column design. Saturation breaks the V∗​ scaling of Example 4.2 for strong lenses; the others change the numbers, not the method.

  2. Show from (4.7) that the lens strength is unchanged when B is scaled by V∗​, and use this to explain Example 4.2.
  3. Using Δrs​=Cs​α3 and Δrd​≈λ/α for diffraction, find the angle at which the two are equal for the default lens at 800 V, and the size of the blur there.

Chapter 5The spot

The probe on the wafer is the source image, blurred by diffraction and by the spherical and chromatic aberration of the objective. This chapter adds the four blurs in the classic way and in the FW50 way of Barth and Kruit, finds the beam angle that makes the probe smallest for an asked current, derives the optimum in closed form where it exists, and checks the result against a published worked example.

5.1Four blurs on one spot

Sunlight focused by a magnifying glass makes a bright dot, but never a point: the dot has a size because the sun is not a point, because the glass is not perfect, and because light is a wave. The probe of an electron column is the same kind of dot, and it is blurred in the same four ways. Each has a picture.

The source image: the lenses form an image of the virtual source of chapter 2, and that image has a size dI​. Diffraction: the electron is a wave of wavelength λ=h/2meV∗​ (chapter 3; V∗ is the relativistically corrected beam voltage, 43.3 pm at 800 V). A wave that converges in a cone of half-angle α carries sideways momentum only up to about pα, and by the uncertainty relation it cannot be squeezed into a region much narrower than h/(pα)=λ/α. Spherical aberration: rays at large angles are focused too strongly (§4.6) and miss the paraxial image by Cs​α3. Chromatic aberration: an electron whose energy differs by ΔE sees a lens of slightly different strength, its focus moves along the axis by Cc​ΔE/(eV∗), and a ray at angle α that crosses the axis that far from the image plane misses it sideways by Cc​αΔE/(eV∗).

The angle α, set by an aperture, decides the balance. A small angle makes the aberrations negligible and the diffraction large; a large angle the reverse. The angle also decides the current. Brightness, the current per area per solid angle, divided by V∗, is the quantity that Liouville's theorem conserves down the column (chapter 3); with the practical brightness Bpr​=Br​/ln2 of chapter 3 (Br​ is the reduced brightness of chapter 2) the probe current is

Ip​=Bpr​V∗4πdI2​​πα2,dI​=π2Bpr​V∗α24Ip​​​.
(5.1)

For a given current, a wider cone needs a smaller source image. The source image is the virtual source times the total magnification of the column, which the condenser lenses set. For chapter 2's cold tip the virtual source is only 1.30 nm across, and 10 pA at 5 mrad needs dI​= 0.812 nm: a total magnification of 0.63, so here the condensers must enlarge the source before the objective's demagnification of 0.018 (chapter 4). With the objective alone the source image would be 0.023 nm and the current 8.3 fA. A cold field emitter's tiny source is spent on current. So the asked current is a knob of the problem, the source-image size follows from it, and the spot size is what we pay.

5.2How the blurs add

The four blurs are not independent shapes that could be laid side by side. The probe is the source image convolved with the blur of a point (diffraction and aberrations together), and a convolution does not add widths in any simple way. Two conventions are in use, and the simulation offers both.

The classic quadrature sum. Each term is given a diameter and the squares are added, as for independent Gaussian errors:

dp2​=(1.22αλ​)2+(21​Cs​α3)2+(Cc​eV∗ΔE​α)2+dI2​.
(5.2)

The diffraction diameter is the Airy disc out to its first dark ring. The spherical term is the disc of least confusion: the narrowest cross-section of the cone of aberrated rays. At the paraxial image the outermost rays miss by Cs​α3, so the blur there is 2Cs​α3 across; a little before it, at Δz=−43​Cs​α2, the bundle is narrowest, 21​Cs​α3 across (check P3 finds both numbers by brute force). The chromatic term is the spread of focus across the energy width ΔE, here the FWHM of chapter 2. The convention is simple and widely taught, and its weakness is known: the terms are not Gaussian, and their diameters are not defined alike (an Airy disc to its first zero holds 84 % of the current; a disc of least confusion holds all of it).

The FW50 root-power sum. Barth and Kruit (Optik 101, 101, 1996) define every term as the diameter that holds half the current (FW50) and combine them by a rule fitted to full wave-optical calculations of probes. In the form of Bronsgeest, Barth, Swanson and Kruit (J. Vac. Sci. Technol. B 26, 949, 2008, Eqs. 18 to 21; open copy):

dp​=((dA4​+dS4​)1.3/4+dI1.3​)2/1.3+dC2​​,
(5.3)
dA​=0.54αλ​,dS​=0.18Cs​α3,dC​=0.6Cc​eV∗ΔE50​​α.
(5.4)

Each term is the FW50 the probe would have if that blur acted alone. We checked two coefficients from first principles: the Airy disc holds half its current inside 0.535 λ/α (check P7; the paper prints its Eq. 19 as 0.66×10−9/(αV​) in metres and volts, which is the same thing, because λV​=1.226 nm·V½), and a spherically aberrated bundle that fills the aperture evenly has its smallest FW50, 0.177 Cs​α3, at Δz=−83​Cs​α2 (check P8). The chromatic coefficient 0.6 we take from the paper. The powers have no derivation: in the paper's words, "the powers are simply those that give a good approximation to complete simulations". What they do is easy to see. Whenever one term is much larger than the others, dp​ tends to it. Diffraction and spherical aberration are added with the power 4, so the larger of the two dominates sharply: both are parts of one wave aberration of the same point image. The source image joins with the power 1.3, a softer sum than quadrature. The chromatic term is added in quadrature.

The ΔE50​ in dC​ is the FW50 of the energy distribution, the narrowest energy interval holding half the electrons; for chapter 2's cold source it is 0.157 eV against a FWHM of 0.215 eV (check P9), and the module takes it from chapter 2. The FW50 is also what a knife-edge measurement relates to most directly: for the three probe shapes Bronsgeest et al. compare (Gaussian, Lorentzian, top hat) the FW50 is 1.76 times the 25–75 % edge width.

Key result · probe size

For an asked current Ip​, the probe diameter is a function of the beam angle alone: diffraction falls as 1/α, the source image as 1/α, chromatic aberration rises as α and spherical aberration as α3. There is one angle at which dp​ is smallest, and the column is run near it.

5.3The best angle

For two terms the best angle can be found by hand. Take diffraction A/α and spherical aberration Bα3 in quadrature. The derivative of A2α−2+B2α6 is −2A2α−3+6B2α5; it vanishes at α8=A2/(3B2) (check P1). With the classic A=1.22λ and B=21​Cs​ this is αopt​= 1.09 (λ/Cs​)1/4 and dmin​= 1.29 λ3/4Cs1/4​: the optimum angle grows only as the fourth root of λ/Cs​, which is why a lens twice as bad costs so little in angle. With diffraction and chromatic aberration Kα, K=Cc​ΔE/(eV∗), the derivative of A2α−2+K2α2 vanishes at α=A/K​, where the diameter is 2AK​ (check P2): the spot scales as the square root of the chromatic coefficient times the relative energy spread.

With all four terms the solver searches for the minimum numerically (golden-section search on lnα between 0.1 and 100 mrad). With the chromatic term and the current switched off it reproduces the closed form of P1 to seven digits, 10.99 mrad for the default lens, and with the spherical term switched off that of P2, 8.318 mrad (checks P4 and P5). The default case is close to the second: at 800 V the optimum is a balance of diffraction against chromatic aberration.

Example 5.1 · the default spot

Chapter 4's objective (Cs​= 4.19 mm, Cc​= 2.85 mm), chapter 2's cold source (Br​= 2.13 × 10⁸ A m−2 sr−1 V−1, ΔE50​= 0.157 eV, FWHM 0.215 eV), landing at 800 V, asking for 10 pA at 5 mrad. In the FW50 convention the parts are dA​= 4.68 nm, dS​= 0.0943 nm, dC​= 1.68 nm and dI​= 0.812 nm, and the probe is dp​= 5.32 nm. Diffraction dominates at this angle. Opening the beam to the optimum, 8.67 mrad, gives 4.11 nm, with diffraction 2.70 nm and chromatic blur 2.91 nm nearly equal and spherical aberration (0.491 nm) and source image (0.468 nm) minor. The classic quadrature sum gives 11.3 nm at 5 mrad and 9.08 nm at its optimum of 8.14 mrad, 2.2 times the FW50 value: the two conventions measure different things, and a specification must say which it means.

Example 5.2 · current against size, and a better lens

At 1 pA the smallest FW50 probe is 4.0 nm (at 8.4 mrad); at 1 nA it is 6.2 nm (at 12 mrad). A thousand times the current costs only a factor 1.5 in size, because the optimum angle opens and the extra current is collected over a wider cone. At 1 nA the chromatic blur (4.04 nm) is still larger than the source image (3.37 nm); the source image becomes the largest part only above about 1.8 nA. An immersion-type objective with Cs​= 0.2 mm and Cc​= 0.1 mm (calculated values of Tsuno et al., 1995, quoted in this project's data) gives 1.1 nm at 10 pA, at 26 mrad: at this current the source image is a minor part, so a better lens is what shrinks the spot.

Example 5.3 · the same column at 30 kV

Landing at 30 kV with the same lens geometry (excited for the higher voltage, chapter 4) gives 0.56 nm at 7.9 mrad for 10 pA. The shorter wavelength and the smaller relative energy spread both help. The price is the deeper and harder hit in the wafer, which chapter 6 measures.

5.4Our lens and spot next to published values

Published aberration coefficients of real objectives (collected with their provenance in data/ch05/objective_lens_cs_cc.csv) run from 0.17 to 5 mm in Cs​. Our bell-field objective, 4.19 and 2.85 mm at a 3 mm working distance, is larger than all but one of the ten published lens values there: about twice the 2 mm that the corrector maker CEOS gives for an uncorrected CD-SEM column (a CD-SEM is the scanning electron microscope that measures critical dimensions, the widths of chip features; chapter 7), and below only Joy's "typical" 5 mm (J. Surf. Sci. Nanotechnol. 4, 369, 2006, for a low-voltage objective at a 4 mm working distance). Magnetic immersion lenses reach a few tenths of a millimetre. The bell field is a teaching model, and its working distance is long by these standards. These are values read from abstracts, excerpts and a manufacturer's table, not measurements we could check. For the spot itself we found no published probe diameter we could compare like for like: manufacturers quote image resolution, a different quantity (Hitachi, for instance, states 0.4 nm at 30 kV for its SU9600 cold-field-emission SEM, manufacturer's page), which is the same order as our 0.56 nm at 30 kV with a lens of several times larger Cs​.

Joy also gives a worked spot size: Cs​=Cc​= 5 mm, 1 keV, a Schottky spread of 0.7 eV, his three terms in quadrature, "about 18 nm" at 4 to 5 mrad. His diffraction term is 0.61λ/α, which is the radius of the Airy disc to its first zero, used beside a diameter for the spherical term; we reproduce his formulas as printed. At 5 mrad they give 18.1 nm, which reproduces his number (check P10). Their smallest value, however, is 12.9 nm at 2.60 mrad; the excerpt we read does not say why 4 to 5 mrad was taken. Bronsgeest et al. also give the current at which source image and diffraction disc are equally large, Ip​= 1.08×10−18 B; their Eqs. 6 and 19 reproduce it (check P6).

Scherzer's theorem (§4.6) is what makes all of this unavoidable: with a round, static lens Cs​ and Cc​ cannot be made zero, so the spot always has an optimum and the optimum is always a compromise. Aberration correctors with multipoles break the theorem's assumptions and shift the optimum to larger angles and more current; they are outside this project.

The browser module physics/ch05.js and ref/ch05.py agree to 10−15 in the closed formulas and to about 10−12 in the optimum angle at the test cases, where the minimum is flat (parity check; at 100 V the two searches part at the ninth digit).

What chapters 7 and 8 receive. The probe diameter dp​ (FW50) and the probe current Ip​, with the angle that produced them.

What the model leaves out. A wave-optical calculation of the probe (the root-power sum is a fit to such calculations). The aberrations of the gun and condensers, which the objective demagnifies but does not remove, and which at large current limit how much of the emission can be used at all; Bronsgeest et al. stop their example at 20 nA for that reason. Coma and astigmatism from misalignment. Fifth-order spherical aberration, which matters at angles of tens of milliradians. The overlap of objective and retarding field of a decelerating column (chapter 4). Coulomb interactions between the electrons in the beam, which blur it at large current (the trajectory-displacement effect); the sliders and the figure run to 10 nA without them. Stage vibration, stray fields and the finite scan step. Each adds to the probe of a real column.
