Chapter 6Scan and hit

What the electrons of the probe do inside the wafer: they turn at the nuclei and slow down among the electrons, and some come back out. We follow them one by one in a Monte Carlo simulation built on the screened Rutherford cross-section and the Bethe stopping power, count the backscattered and secondary electrons, measure how far the electrons wander, and compare the counts with a database of measurements and with published simulations.

6.1Into the wafer

Throw a handful of marbles into a box of loosely packed heavier balls. Each marble rattles about, changes direction at every hit, and slows down; some bounce back out of the box, the rest come to rest inside. An electron entering a wafer does the same, with two kinds of collision. It is deflected by the atomic nuclei, which are far heavier than it is (51000 times for silicon, 3.6 × 10⁵ times for gold): such a hit turns it while taking away at most four times the mass ratio of its energy, about one part in 10 000 for silicon, an elastic collision. And it loses energy to the electrons of the solid in many small bites, ionising and exciting as it goes, inelastic collisions, which hardly turn it.

What comes back out is the signal of the microscope. Electrons that turn round and leave with most of their energy are backscattered electrons (BSE); their number per incident electron is the backscattering coefficient η. The energy the beam leaves in the solid frees slow electrons of a few electronvolts, and those born within a few nanometres of the surface can escape: secondary electrons (SE), by convention those leaving with less than 50 eV; their number per incident electron is the yield δ. A secondary electron made by the incoming beam right where it enters carries the sharp information; one made by a backscattered electron on its way out comes from wherever that electron surfaced, which can be far from the beam. How far the electrons wander, and how many come back, is what this chapter computes, for the probe of chapter 5 landing on silicon, aluminium, copper or gold.

No closed formula follows hundreds of random turns. We follow the electrons one by one instead, drawing each turn and each free path from the probability laws of the two collisions: a Monte Carlo simulation, in the form D. C. Joy describes (Scanning Microscopy 5, 329, 1991), with the secondary-electron model of Y. Lin and D. C. Joy (Surf. Interface Anal. 37, 895, 2005).

6.2Scanning the probe

To make an image the probe is moved over the wafer line by line, as the spot of an old television tube was. A pair of deflection coils above the objective tilts the beam by a small angle, and the lens turns that tilt into a sideways shift on the wafer. The physics is chapter 1's: an electron of momentum p that crosses a transverse magnetic field B over a length ℓ leaves turned by the small angle θ=eBℓ/p, because the sideways force evB acts for the time ℓ/v and gives the sideways momentum eBℓ. With the pivot of the deflection a distance L above the wafer, the spot moves by Lθ.

Example 6.1 · how much field a scan needs

To sweep a field of view of 1 µm, half of it on each side, with the pivot 3 mm above the wafer, the beam must turn by 0.17 mrad. At 800 V a deflector 5 mm long does that with B=θp/(eℓ)= 3.2 µT, a field smaller than the Earth's, which is some tens of microtesla. That is why electron columns are shielded with soft iron and why stray fields from the fab blur images: a field the size of the scan field, varying in time, moves the spot as much as the scan does.

Each point of the scan is a pixel, held for the dwell time td​; chapter 7 counts the electrons that a pixel returns. This chapter asks what happens to the beam electrons at one point.

6.3Turning: the screened Rutherford cross-section

An electron passing a nucleus of charge Ze is pulled by the Coulomb force and leaves turned by an angle φ. Rutherford's calculation of this two-body problem gives the probability of a turn into the solid angle dΩ as an effective target area, the differential cross-section. For a fast electron of momentum p and speed v it is

dΩdσ​=(4πε0​Ze2​)2(pv)21​(1−cosφ)21​,
(6.1)

which in the non-relativistic case, pv=2E, is the textbook form with sin4(φ/2) in the denominator. ★ It follows from the orbit. An electron that would pass the nucleus at the distance b (the impact parameter) if it were not deflected is turned by φ with tan(φ/2)=k/(pvb), k=Ze2/4πε0​, the hyperbola of the Kepler problem: the nucleus attracts the electron as the Sun attracts a passing comet, and the deflection obeys the same formula as for the repelled alpha particles of Rutherford. The electrons that pass through the ring between b and b+db, of area 2πbdb, leave into the cone between φ and φ+dφ, of solid angle 2πsinφdφ; so dσ/dΩ=b∣db/dφ∣/sinφ, which with b=(k/pv)cot(φ/2) is (6.1) (check M2). The formula diverges at small angles because a bare Coulomb field reaches to infinity. In a solid the atom's own electrons screen the nucleus beyond about an atomic radius, which removes the divergence. Joy, following Bishop (1976), writes the screening as a shift of the denominator to (1−cosφ+2a)2, with the screening parameter

a=3.4×10−3E/keVZ0.67​,
(6.2)

fitted so that simulated backscattering agrees with experiment. Integrating the screened form over all directions (check M1),

∫(1−cosφ+2a)2dΩ​=2π∫02​(u+2a)2du​=a(1+a)π​,u=1−cosφ,

gives the total elastic cross-section, and with pv=E(E+2mc2)/(E+mc2) (check M3)

σE​=(4πε0​Ze2​)2a(1+a)π​E21​(E+2mc2E+mc2​)2.
(6.3)

Joy's Eq. 1 writes the same with numbers, E in keV:

σE​=5.21×10−21E2Z2​a(1+a)4π​(E+1024E+511​)2 cm2.
(6.4)

The constant follows from (e2/4πε0​)2/4= 5.18×10−21 keV2 cm2, and the 4 cancels the quarter that ((E+511)/(E+1022))2 tends to at low energy. Joy prints 5.21 (half a per cent higher, check M3) and 1024 for 2mc2=1022 keV (0.4 % lower in σE​ at low energy); the two nearly cancel, and we use his numbers as printed. A beam crossing a solid with n=NA​ρ/A atoms per volume (ρ the density, A the molar mass, NA​ Avogadro's number) meets a nucleus on average once per elastic mean free path

λel​=NA​ρσE​A​.
(6.5)

In silicon it is 1.0 nm at 800 eV, 35 nm at 30 keV and 105 nm at 100 keV. The angle at each hit is mostly small: for silicon at 800 eV the screening parameter is a few hundredths, and half of the turns are smaller than about 2a​ radians. In gold at 800 eV the formula gives 0.091 nm, less than the spacing between gold atoms, 0.26 nm: there the picture of separate collisions with single atoms has lost its meaning, and the model is a parametrisation rather than a description.

How good is this cross-section? Rutherford's formula treats the electron as a classical particle in a point-charge field and ignores its spin; Bishop's screening parameter was fitted to measured backscattering, so agreement with backscattering data is partly built in. A measure of how strong the nucleus's field is for the passing electron is the Sommerfeld parameter Zαfs​/β (αfs​ the fine-structure constant, β=v/c); the simple treatments of the screened field need it small. At 800 eV it is 1.8 for silicon and 10 for gold. For heavy elements and low energies the proper replacement is the Mott cross-section from the Dirac equation; in Joy's words, "at such low energies the Rutherford cross-section is not accurate and a Mott cross-section must be used". He also states plainly that his models "are not, in principle, suitable for incident beam energies below 1 keV". Our default, 800 eV, is below that. We use the model anyway, because it is open and simple, and we measure its error against data in §6.6.

6.4Slowing down: the stopping power

Between the elastic turns the electron loses energy to the electrons of the solid. A single loss is usually tens of electronvolts, small against keV, and there are many of them per mean free path. Joy therefore lets the energy fall continuously along the path, at the rate given by Bethe's stopping power. In the low-energy form of Joy and Luo, which Lin and Joy use (their Eq. 13, written here per length, with the density),

−dsdE​=78500AEρZ​ln(J1.166(E+kJ)​) cmkeV​,k=0.85,
(6.6)

with ρ in g cm−3, A in g mol−1 and E in keV. The picture behind Bethe's formula is a fast charge sweeping past the atomic electrons: each feels a short electric pulse and takes up momentum, the more the slower the charge passes, hence the 1/E. The numbers are not arbitrary: 78500≈2π(e2/4πε0​)2NA​= 78500 keV2 cm2 mol−1, and 1.166=e/2​ with e=2.718… (check M8). The logarithm counts the range of distances over which the pulse is short enough to excite an electron of typical binding energy J, the mean ionisation energy; Joy's Eq. 12 (Berger and Seltzer) gives it as J=(9.76Z+58.5Z−0.19) eV, 172 eV for silicon and 797 eV for gold, within 3 % of the values NIST uses (check M7). The term kJ is Joy and Luo's empirical change: without it the logarithm turns negative below E=J/1.166, which is meaningless; with it the logarithm stays positive down to E=(1/1.166−k)J, about 1 eV for silicon and 6 eV for gold, far below the 50 eV at which we stop following an electron, and by their measurements it fits stopping powers down to about 50 eV (D. C. Joy et al., Scanning Microscopy 10, 1996, Table 2 gives fitted k of 0.795 for silicon and 0.832 for gold; we keep 0.85, the value Lin and Joy used with their secondary-electron constants).

Treating the loss as continuous needs many small losses between two elastic turns. At 800 eV in silicon the loss per elastic mean free path is only 22 eV, about one plasmon (the collective oscillation of the valence electrons, 16.6 eV for silicon's four valence electrons per atom in the free-electron model). At the default the continuous loss is therefore an average over a few events, one more approximation of the model at low energy. At 30 keV the elastic steps are long and hold hundreds of losses.

The NIST table ESTAR lists the stopping power computed from the full relativistic Bethe theory. The comparison (table below, check M7; ESTAR gives the stopping power per areal density, so we divide ours by the density): from 5 to 30 keV the two agree to between 0.93 and 1.05. Below, Joy–Luo is larger, up to 2.3 times for gold at 1 keV, where Bethe's theory itself is no longer valid and neither number is a measurement. Above, Joy–Luo falls behind (0.78 at 100 keV) because it is non-relativistic: the true stopping power goes as 1/β2, not as 1/E, and β2/(2E/mc2)= 0.77 at 100 keV. The chapter's range ends at 30 keV, inside the band of agreement.

6.5The Monte Carlo loop

Each electron starts at the point of impact, heading straight into the wafer with the landing energy E. Then the same four steps repeat.

1. A free path. The chance of travelling a distance s without an elastic hit falls as e−s/λel​, the law of a constant hazard. A path with this distribution is s=−λel​lnξ1​, with ξ1​ a random number uniform between 0 and 1: the fraction of paths longer than s is the fraction of ξ1​ below e−s/λel​ (check M4). Ten per cent of the paths are longer than 2.3λel​.

2. A move and a loss. The electron moves s along its direction and loses s∣dE/ds∣ by (6.6). If the step would take it above the surface, it is cut there: the electron has left the wafer, and it counts as backscattered if its energy is still above 50 eV. If the loss would take its energy below 50 eV, the step is cut where that happens and the electron stops.

3. A turn. The polar angle of the elastic hit comes from the same trick applied to the angular distribution. The fraction of hits that turn by less than φ is, from the integral above, F(φ)=(1+a)(1−cosφ)/(1−cosφ+2a); setting it equal to a second random number ξ2​ and solving for cosφ gives Joy's Eq. 6 (check M1),

cosφ=1−1+a−ξ2​2aξ2​​,
(6.7)

while the azimuth about the old direction is uniform, ψ=2πξ3​.

4. A new direction. The unit vector of motion is turned by φ and ψ about itself. Joy's formulas divide by the direction cosine cz​ and fail for an electron moving exactly parallel to the surface; we use the equivalent rotation c′=ccosφ+sinφ(e^1​cosψ+e^2​sinψ) with two unit vectors e^1,2​ perpendicular to c, built from c without that division. Check M5 confirms on 20 000 cases, random ones, directions parallel to the surface and directions along and near each axis, that the new vector has unit length and makes exactly the angle φ with the old one.

The loop runs until the electron leaves or stops. The page runs 2000 electrons for each setting, each with its own stream of pseudo-random numbers (the 32-bit generator mulberry32, seeded per electron), so the same settings always give the same numbers, and the Python reference ref/ch06.py reproduces the browser's numbers from the same streams (parity check: the readouts agree to about 10−13, the drawn paths to about 10−9, from last-bit differences of library functions). One setting takes up to a second at 30 kV, so the readouts follow the slider with a delay.

How sure is a count of 2000? Whether a given electron comes back is a coin with probability η; for N electrons the count has the binomial standard deviation, so the estimate η^​ carries the standard error uη​=η(1−η)/N​. For δ the spread of the individual electrons' contributions gives uδ​ in the same way. Both are readouts of the simulation, and the text quotes them. The lateral spread σs​ below has no error estimate of its own; it is set by a few electrons that surface far away, so it fluctuates more than η and δ do.

Key result · what one simulated electron needs

Two probability laws and one rate: free paths s=−λel​lnξ from the screened Rutherford cross-section, turns cosφ=1−2aξ/(1+a−ξ), and a continuous loss ∣dE/ds∣ from the Bethe–Joy–Luo stopping power. The statistical error of every count falls as 1/N​.

6.6What comes back: η and δ

Backscattering. The simulated η is compared in Figure 6.1 with the measurements collected by Akbari et al. (an open database, CC BY 4.0; data/ch06/README.md gives its provenance). For silicon and aluminium the agreement is within the spread of the measurements at all energies, also below 1 keV, where Joy warns that the model is not meant to work; recall that the screening parameter was fitted to backscattering data, so this agreement is partly by construction: between 0.4 and 2 keV the simulation gives 0.24 for silicon and the 5 measurements average 0.24. For the heavy elements the model is too generous. Gold backscatters 0.55 in the simulation against 0.49 measured between 8 and 31 keV, and 0.66 against 0.34 between 0.4 and 2 keV; copper lies between (0.41 against 0.31 at low energy). For gold even the trend is wrong: the measured η rises with energy, the simulated one falls. That is the failure Joy predicts for low energy and high Z, where the Rutherford cross-section is not accurate, and where the Sommerfeld parameter above is large. So the model is fair for silicon and aluminium and overstates the backscattering of copper and gold, most at low energy (check M11 records all bands).

Secondary electrons. Lin and Joy model the secondary yield in two steps (their Eqs. 1 to 3). Energy lost by the beam makes secondaries at the rate ε1​∣dE/ds∣ per path length, where ε is the mean energy spent per secondary electron, and a secondary born at depth z escapes with probability 21​e−z/λs​: half of them start towards the surface, and on the way they are absorbed with the escape depth λs​. Lin and Joy fitted ε and λs​ to the measured yield curves of each element with their own Monte Carlo (their Table 1: silicon 90 eV and 2.7 nm, gold 35 eV and 0.5 nm). We add these escape weights along every step of every electron, exactly for each straight piece (check M6), on the way in and on the way out; so δ counts both the secondaries made by the incoming beam and those made by the backscattered electrons leaving.

Lin and Joy also give a universal law (their Eq. 12) that describes measured yield curves of all elements by two numbers, the largest yield δmax​ and the energy Emax​ at which it occurs:

δmax​δ​=1.28(Emax​E​)−0.67[1−exp(−1.614(Emax​E​)1.67)]
(6.8)

(silicon 0.89 at 450 eV, gold 1.28 at 500 eV, their Table 1). Figure 6.2 compares our simulation with this law and with the values of their own Monte Carlo at 2 and 20 keV. At 800 eV in silicon the simulation gives δ= 0.76 ± 0.009 and the law 0.76: they agree. For gold at 800 eV ours is 29 % above the law, and above their δmax​. At 20 keV ours is below their Monte Carlo for every element (0.048 against 0.080 for silicon, 0.17 against 0.37 for gold, check M12), while for gold it is 25 % above their law, which their own Monte Carlo exceeds by more still. The simulations share ε, λs​ and the equations the paper states; the paper does not give the rest of their simulation, so we cannot say where the difference comes from, and we record it rather than tune it away.

Example 6.2 · silicon at 800 V

The default probe lands with 800 eV on silicon. Of 2000 simulated electrons a fraction η= 0.25 ± 0.01 comes back as backscattered electrons, and each incident electron frees on average δ= 0.76 ± 0.009 secondary electrons. For silicon δ+η= 1.0: in this model 800 V is almost exactly the voltage at which as many electrons leave as arrive, so an insulating surface would hardly charge; measured crossover voltages depend on the surface and we did not compare them. Gold at the same voltage gives η= 0.67 and δ= 1.5, together 2.2, both too high by the comparisons above. The model itself has no charging, and conductive silicon and gold drain any charge to ground.

6.7How far the electrons go

The classic estimate of how deep electrons go is the range of K. Kanaya and S. Okayama (J. Phys. D 5 (1972) 43; we use the formula as Goldstein et al. quote it, not the original),

RKO​=27.6Z0.89ρAE1.67​ nm
(6.9)

with A in g mol−1, ρ in g cm−3 and E in keV. The power 1.67 is the integral of the stopping power: with ∣dE/ds∣∝1/E (ignoring the slow logarithm) the path to stop grows as E2, and the logarithm and the scattering bring the exponent down. The range grows almost as the square of the energy. That is the whole case for low-voltage metrology in one line.

From the simulation we take two more measures. The radius r90​ of the hemisphere about the point of impact that holds 90 % of the energy left in the wafer, and the interaction volume Vint​=32​πr903​ defined by it. And the lateral spread σs​ of the secondary-electron signal: the root mean square distance, along one direction across the surface, of the points where escaping secondaries are born, weighted by their escape probability. It is what blurs an edge in the image beyond the size of the probe. One root-mean-square number describes a two-part signal poorly: a sharp core of secondaries made where the beam enters, and a broad halo made by backscattered electrons surfacing far away. The halo sets σs​, so at high voltage σs​ overstates the blur of the sharp part. We therefore also split the signal. From a weighted histogram of where the escaping secondaries are born, the core width σcore​ is the median distance divided by 0.67449 (the ratio for a Gaussian), the core fraction fcore​ is the share of the signal within three core widths, and the halo width σhalo​ is the root-mean-square distance of the rest. The model lets a secondary escape where it is born; its own sideways travel on the way out, of the order of the escape depth λs​, is added to the core width in quadrature, σcore2​=(median width)2+λs2​, a rough allowance rather than a transport calculation. Chapter 7 blurs edges with the two parts separately.

Example 6.3 · 800 V against 30 kV in silicon

At 800 V the Kanaya–Okayama range is 22 nm, 90 % of the energy stays within 14 nm of the point of impact, and the secondary signal spreads with σs​= 3.9 nm: 86 % of it in a core of 3.3 nm, the rest in a halo of 8.7 nm, all of the order of the probe of chapter 5. At 30 kV the range is 9.3 µm, r90​= 6.6 µm, and σs​= 1.4 µm: the interaction volume is about 1 × 10⁸ times larger, and the root-mean-square spread 360 times wider. The split shows what that number hides: 62 % of the signal is still in a core of 2.7 nm, set by the escape depth because the incoming beam has not yet scattered sideways in the top nanometres, and the rest is a halo of 2.2 µm, made by backscattered electrons surfacing micrometres away. The halo lowers the contrast; the core keeps the edges sharp. Meanwhile the beam deposits its energy deep in the device, and the beam deposits its energy deep in the device. At low voltage both the halo and the damage are confined to the top tens of nanometres.

Example 6.4 · gold at 800 V

In gold the range at 800 V is only 4.0 nm: the dense, heavy target stops and turns the electrons quickly. The simulation then sends back 0.67 of them, which is too many by the comparison above; a design decision that rests on the backscatter of a heavy metal at low voltage needs the Mott cross-section.

What chapter 7 receives. The secondary yield δ, the backscattering coefficient η and the spread of the signal as core width, core fraction and halo width, for the material and voltage chosen, with their statistical errors.

What the model leaves out. The Mott cross-section, which heavy elements at low energy need (shown above). Discrete energy losses (plasmons, inner-shell ionisation) and the energy spectrum of the backscattered electrons. The transport of the secondary electrons themselves, replaced by Lin and Joy's exponential escape. Charging of insulators, which at low voltage decides the contrast of resist and oxide. Compounds: no resist, no oxide, no layered stack, although the database has resist data. Above all, topography: the wafer here is flat, while a metrology tool looks at lines and edges, where secondaries escape through the side walls and the yield rises at the edge; chapter 7 models the edge as a signal profile instead. And the crystal: channelling in single-crystal silicon changes backscattering with the angle of incidence.

  3. Run the simulation for silicon from 0.5 to 5 kV and plot δ+η. At which voltage does it cross one, and what would that mean for an insulating sample?

Chapter 7Detect and measure

The probe is scanned across a pattern of lines, and a width is read from the electrons that come back. We build the expected profile from the secant law and the blurs of chapters 5 and 6, add the shot noise of the beam and the randomness of the secondary yield, read the width with a threshold rule, and find how its scatter depends on current, time and dose, checked by error propagation and by Monte Carlo.

7.1Reading a width from an image

A metrology tool in a chip factory does one thing over and over: it puts the probe of chapter 5 on a pattern, scans it across in lines, counts the electrons that come back for each point, and reads a width, the critical dimension (CD), from the resulting picture. A good picture needs many electrons per point; a factory needs many measurements per hour; and the wafer must not be damaged by the beam. This chapter turns those three demands into numbers for the simplest pattern there is, a row of parallel lines.

The lines in an electron image look like their own outlines: bright edges on a duller ground. Figure 7.1 shows why. Secondary electrons escape only from a thin layer under the surface, of thickness about the escape depth λs​ of chapter 6. A beam that hits a flat surface crosses that layer on a path of length λs​; one that hits a wall tilted by θ crosses it on the longer path λs​/cosθ and frees proportionally more secondaries that can get out. The yield grows as 1/cosθ, the secant law, and on a near-vertical wall it is many times the flat value.

7.2The expected profile

Across one period p of the pattern, a line of width CD at half its height h stands on the floor; its walls lean by the angle β from the vertical, so each wall covers the width w=htanβ seen from above. On the flat top and floor the yield is chapter 6's δ. On a wall the surface is tilted by θ=90∘−β, and the secant law gives δ/sinβ. The excess over the flat value, summed across one wall, is

δ(sinβ1​−1)htanβ=δh(cosβ1​−tanβ),
(7.1)

which stays finite for a vertical wall, where it becomes δh (check C3): a vertical wall is invisible in projection, yet it adds as much signal as a flat strip of width h. Backscattered electrons add a flat η, because we give them no dependence on the slope.

The detector never sees this sharp map. The probe has a size, and the signal spreads in the solid before it escapes. We treat both as Gaussian blurs. A round Gaussian probe of FW50 diameter dp​ has the standard deviation σp​=dp​/2.355 along any line (check C2). Chapter 6 splits the escaping secondaries into a core, a fraction fcore​ of width σcore​ made by the incoming beam, and a halo of width σhalo​ made by backscattered electrons. Each part is blurred by its own Gaussian, σ12​=σp2​+σcore2​ and σ22​=σp2​+σhalo2​. The expected yield at the beam position x is then the flat value plus each wall's excess spread over its width and blurred,

Y(x)=δ+η+walls∑​wδh(1/cosβ−tanβ)​k=1,2∑​fk​[Φ(σk​x−x1​​)−Φ(σk​x−x2​​)],
(7.2)

with f1​=fcore​, f2​=1−fcore​, x1​ and x2​ the ends of a wall in projection and Φ the cumulative normal distribution (the error function, approximated to 1.5×10−7 by formula 7.1.26 of M. Abramowitz and I. A. Stegun, Handbook of Mathematical Functions, 1964, check C4). The pattern is periodic, so the walls of the neighbouring lines are added too (two neighbouring periods on each side when the blur is small, more when it is wide; a halo wider than twice the pitch is simply a uniform background): at a pitch of 40 nm and a blur of a few nanometres they overlap.

The default numbers are chapter 6's silicon at 800 V, rounded: δ=0.76, η=0.24, a core of 3.3 nm holding 86 % of the signal and a halo of 8.7 nm (the core includes the escape depth λs​=2.7 nm), and chapter 5's probe of 5.3 nm, so σ1​= 4.0 nm. The line is 20 nm wide and 30 nm high (aspect ratio 1.5), the space 20 nm, and the core blur is 0.20 of the space: the edges are sharp enough to find, but the neighbours' edges already lift the floor.

A Gaussian is a fair stand-in for the probe. For each part of the signal it is rougher, and the split into two parts is itself a summary of chapter 6's histogram, not its full shape.

7.3Counting electrons

Electrons arrive one by one. A current of Ip​ held on a pixel for the dwell time td​ brings on average nˉ=Ip​td​/e electrons, and the actual number fluctuates from pixel to pixel by the Poisson law, with variance equal to the mean. This is shot noise, and it is where the graininess of charge, a quantum fact, enters the measurement. Each beam electron then frees a random number of secondaries, of which a fraction ηc​ reaches the detector. If that number is also Poisson, with mean m=ηc​Y, the counts k of one pixel have

⟨k⟩=nˉm,Vark=nˉ(m+m2)
(7.3)

by the law of total variance (check C1): the beam's own shot noise is amplified by the random yield. Whether secondaries really follow Poisson statistics we did not verify against a measurement; it is the simplest assumption and is stated as such. (Backscattered electrons are counted the same way, although each beam electron gives at most one; that adds about 1.3 % to the variance at the default.)

A useful single number is the contrast-to-noise ratio of one scan line, SNR=(⟨kedge​⟩−⟨kfloor​⟩)/Varkfloor​​: how far the bright edge stands out of the noise of the floor, in one line of the raw image.

Example 7.1 · one line of the default image

With 10 pA and 100 ns per pixel, each pixel receives nˉ= 6.2 electrons. On a 1 nm pixel that is a dose of 100 µC cm−2 per image, the order of the dose that exposes an electron-beam resist, which is why resists shrink under a metrology beam. With the collection fraction 0.5, one scan line has SNR= 2.0: the edges stand out of the noise by only a few standard deviations. The tool averages the 512 lines of the image along the line direction into one profile: 3200 beam electrons land on each position across the line, and the detector counts the fraction ηc​Y of them.

The collection fraction ηc​ is a property of the detector. Applied Materials states publicly that the Elluminator detector of its PROVision 10 system "captures 95% of back-scattered electrons" (product page, read 9 November 2026). We quote that as the company's claim (the page was re-read on that date); it concerns backscattered, not secondary, electrons, and it is not an input of this model, whose default 0.5 is an assumption.

7.4Finding the edges

The averaged profile is still noisy, and the width must be read from it by a rule. We use a simple and common one, a threshold on the outer flank of each edge peak. The floor level Sfloor​ is the mean of the pixels in the middle half of the space; the level of each edge peak is the mean of the three pixels around its maximum; the threshold is half-way between them; and the edge is the point where the profile, followed outwards from the peak, first falls below the threshold, interpolated linearly between pixels. The measured width is the distance between the two edges found.

A rule reads a width, but not necessarily the true one. With a vanishingly small probe and no spread of the signal, the outer flanks are the bottom corners of the line, and the rule finds 21.04 nm against the bottom width 21.05 nm (check C7). With the default blur the flanks move outwards and the rule reads 28.2 nm for a line whose true CD is 20 nm: a bias of 8.2 nm, made of the sidewall's projection (the bottom is wider than the middle) and above all of the blur, which moves the half-height point of each outer flank outwards by about one σ1​. The fin-like line of Example 7.3 reads 9.0 nm too wide, 60 % of its width. Such a bias is not an error of the tool but a property of the method; real tools calibrate it away against a reference measurement (cross-section electron microscopy or atomic force microscopy) for each kind of pattern. What cannot be calibrated away is the scatter from one measurement to the next.

7.5The precision of a width

Each pixel of the averaged profile carries the variance (7.3) divided by the number of lines averaged, N. The measured width is a function of all pixel values, CDm​=f(S1​,…,Sn​); to first order in the noise its variance is

σCD2​=i∑​(∂Si​∂f​)2NVarNi​​,
(7.4)

where the derivatives tell how much the found width moves when one pixel goes up by one count. Many of them are zero: only the pixels at the two threshold crossings, those that set the peak levels and those of the floor take part. Near a crossing the derivative is 1/∣S′∣, the inverse slope of the profile there, so steep edges give precise widths. The module takes the derivatives by perturbing each pixel of the noise-free profile and running the rule again.

Error propagation is only first order. To check it, the module also repeats the whole measurement 4000 times on noisy profiles and takes the standard deviation of the widths found (about 1 % statistical error). At the default the two give 0.23 and 0.26 nm; at five settings where the edges stand well out of the floor they agree within 20 % (check C6). The differences come from steps the linear theory cannot see: noise makes the maximum of a sharp edge peak jump between neighbouring pixels, which moves the threshold, and the crossing can move from one pair of pixels to the next. Where the edge contrast is low the two part more, in either direction: for the blunt probe of Example 7.4 the propagation gives 1.8 nm and the Monte Carlo 1.6 nm. Below 5 % contrast the module stops, because the rule then finds no stable edges.

Every term in (7.4) scales as 1/(nˉN), so

σCD​∝Ip​td​N​1​,
(7.5)

the 1/N​ law of counting statistics (check C5 finds the slope −0.500 against the dwell time). Precision is bought with electrons, and electrons cost time and dose.

Key result · precision against time and dose

At a fixed pixel size and pattern, the scatter of a measured width falls as the inverse square root of the number of electrons used, σCD​∝(Ip​td​N)−1/2. Halving it needs four times the electrons. Through the dwell time or the current that is four times the dose on each pixel; through more lines it is four times the scan time at the same dose, because each line falls on fresh wafer.

Example 7.2 · ten times the dwell

At 1 µs per pixel instead of 100 ns, σCD​ falls from 0.23 to 0.072 nm, a factor 3.16, close to 10​; one line's SNR rises to 6.4. The dose rises to 1000 µC cm−2 and the measurements per hour fall to 2900.

Example 7.3 · a fin-like line

A taller, narrower line with vertical walls (15 nm wide, 50 nm high) has brighter edges, by (7.1): one line's SNR is 4.1, the width reads 24.0 nm, and σCD​= 0.16 nm.

Example 7.4 · a blunter probe

A probe of 15 nm instead of chapter 5's 5.3 nm, at the same current, softens the edges: the default line then reads 29.0 nm (a bias of 9.0 nm against 8.2 nm) and its scatter grows from 0.23 to 1.8 nm. The bias changes little, because the neighbours' edges already set it; the precision suffers most.

7.6Measurements per hour

One image of 512 by 512 pixels at 100 ns per pixel takes 26 ms. A measurement site also needs a stage move, focusing and pattern recognition, which we lump into an overhead tov​; we assume 1 s, not a vendor's number. For a square image of N lines of N pixels each (the lines averaged are the rows of the image), the rate is then

N˙m​=N2td​+tov​1​,
(7.6)

3500 per hour at the default, of which the scan itself would allow 1.4 × 10⁵. The overhead dominates, so a faster scan alone gains little; what pays is measuring many features in one image.

Applied Materials states that its PROVision 10 makes "up to 100 million accurate, actionable measurements per hour" with a cold-field-emission column (product page, as above). We cannot check that claim and do not model that tool. As arithmetic only: 100 million per hour is one measurement every 36 µs. In the time of one default image, 26 ms, that is 730 measurements, which is possible only if each image yields hundreds of widths at once, many lines in a large field, read by software in parallel. Our single-line model counts one width per image, so its rate and the claim measure different things.

What chapter 8 receives. The precision σCD​, the bias of the rule, the dose and the measurements per hour, as functions of every input of chapters 2 to 7.

What the model leaves out. A three-dimensional simulation of the electrons in the actual line (the secant law and two Gaussian blurs replace it). The roughness of real line edges, which makes the width vary along the line; averaging 512 lines then measures the mean width, and the scatter of the width along the line is a property of the sample, not noise. Charging, which at low voltage changes the contrast of insulating lines. Shrinkage of resist under the dose of Example 7.1. Detector physics: energy filtering, the geometry of in-lens and side detectors, the analogue noise of the detector chain, and backscattered-electron contrast that depends on the slope. Edge physics beyond the secant law: the law fails near grazing incidence, secondaries escape through two faces near a corner (the edge effect), the trench walls shadow the detector, and line and substrate of different materials give different yields. Smarter rules (fitting a model profile, as real tools do), which are more precise than a threshold. The Gaussian approximation of the noise in the Monte Carlo, which needs many counts per averaged pixel.

Problems
  1. Show that for a threshold crossing on a straight flank of slope S′, with noise σS​ at the crossing and a fixed threshold, the edge scatters by σS​/∣S′∣, so a width with two such edges by 2​σS​/∣S′∣. The module gives less at the default; explain the two effects that move it, one downwards (interpolation between two pixels averages their noise) and one upwards (the threshold itself is set from noisy pixels).
  2. From (7.5) and (7.6), show that at a required σCD​ the product td​N is fixed, so the time per site is N⋅(td​N)+tov​, smallest for the fewest lines with the longest dwell. Name two things that stop a real tool from going to that limit.
  3. With the simulation, find the probe current at which σCD​ reaches 0.1 nm at the default settings with the probe size held fixed, and the dose that costs. Why would the answer be larger in a real column (chapter 5)?

Sources. Applied Materials, PROVision 10 product page, appliedmaterials.com, read 9 November 2026 (claims quoted, nothing modelled on them). M. Abramowitz, I. A. Stegun, Handbook of Mathematical Functions (1964), formula 7.1.26 for the error function. The yields and the escape depth come from chapter 6 and its sources (Joy 1991; Lin and Joy 2005). The secant law and the threshold rule are standard; we did not take them from a particular book, and the model built from them is ours.

Chapter 8The whole machine

Chapters 2 to 7 connected into one chain, from the tip to the precision of a width and the measurements per hour. We ask which inputs matter most (a table of normalised sensitivities), how much the ordinary wobbles of a real machine spread the result (a tolerance Monte Carlo), and which settings meet a specification (a measurement window), and we check the chain against the separate chapters.

8.1One chain from tip to number

Each chapter so far answered one question with the others held fixed. A machine is more like a long train of gears: a small slip at the first gear is passed on, magnified or damped, to the last. A real column is one chain: the tip sets the brightness and the energy spread, the lens sets the aberrations, together they set the probe, the landing voltage sets what the electrons do in the wafer, and all of it decides how precisely a width can be measured and how fast. Turn one knob and everything downstream moves. This chapter connects the chain and asks three questions of it: which inputs matter most, how much the ordinary wobbles of a real machine spread the result, and which settings meet a specification at all.

The simulation at the end of this chapter is the whole machine. Its sliders are the inputs of the earlier chapters, and its numbers come from their own modules, called in a chain: chapter 2 gives the brightness Br​, the FW50 energy spread ΔE50​ and the virtual source size dv​; chapter 4 gives Cs​ and Cc​ for the lens geometry; chapter 5 gives the smallest probe and its angle, because the aperture is always set to the best angle αopt​; chapter 6 gives the yields and the spread of the signal; chapter 7 gives the precision σCD​, the dose and the rate. Only chapter 6 is not rerun: its Monte Carlo takes up to a second per setting, so the chain reads the stored runs behind chapter 6's figures (2000 electrons per point between 0.5 and 30 kV) and interpolates between them.

Example 8.1 · the default machine

Chapter 2's cold tip, chapter 4's lens, landing at 800 V on silicon with 10 pA: the best angle is 8.67 mrad and the probe 4.11 nm. The secondary yield is 0.75, 86 % of it in the sharp core. A 20 nm line, imaged with 100 ns per pixel and averaged over 512 lines, reads 28.0 nm with σCD​= 0.20 nm, at a dose of 100 µC cm−2 and 3500 measurements per hour. These numbers equal those of the separate chapters with the same inputs (check W1); the yield comes from the stored runs of chapter 6, 0.75 against 0.757 ± 0.009 from a fresh run at 800 V, within the statistics of both (check W2).

8.2Which inputs matter: the sensitivity table

A good way to see what matters is to change one input by one per cent and watch each output. The ratio of the relative changes,

Syx​=yx​∂x∂y​=∂lnx∂lny​,
(8.1)

is the normalised sensitivity. It has no unit, so inputs of different kinds can be compared on one scale: S=−0.5 means that one per cent more of the input gives half a per cent less of the output, and S=16 means sixteen per cent more. For a power law y∝xn it is just the exponent n. The module takes it by central differences of ±1 % in each input; the table holds the values at the defaults, ten inputs against four outputs (dp​ the probe, I the probe current with the condensers left at their setting, σCD​ the precision, rate the measurements per hour).

extraction voltage0.3416−8.00

landing voltage−0.7500.470
probe current asked0.0231.0−0.490
working distance0.4400.150
lens half-width0.06700.0220
dwell time00−0.50−0.026
lines averaged00−0.50−0.051
collection fraction00−0.230

Three things stand out. First, the source. With the optics fixed, the probe current answers the tip radius with −15 and the extraction voltage with 16: the field at the apex is Vex​/(krt​), and field emission rises with the field almost as steeply as an exponential (chapter 2). A tip that blunts by one per cent loses 14 % of its current. It follows that such a gun is best run with its emission current held constant by adjusting the extraction voltage as the tip changes (an inference from this table; this project has no source describing a particular gun's control), and that the tip's history matters. Through the number of electrons, the same sensitivity reaches the precision: σCD​ answers the tip radius with 7.5.

Second, the precision follows the counting law of chapter 7 exactly: −0.5 for the dwell time and for the number of lines (check W5), −0.49 for the current, slightly above −0.5 because a larger current also enlarges the probe a little. The landing voltage enters with 0.47: a higher voltage widens the core and the halo of the secondary signal and lowers the yield, which together soften the edges, while the probe shrinks and pulls the other way. The probe itself answers the landing voltage with −0.750, which is the V−3/4 law of a balance of diffraction against chromatic aberration: the diameter goes as AK​ with A∝λ∝V−1/2 and K∝ΔE/V (chapter 5; check W6). It answers the working distance with 0.44. The collection fraction enters the precision with −0.23, smaller in size than the −0.5 of a pure count, because the noise of the counts includes the random yield of secondaries, which collecting more of them does not reduce.

Third, the rate hardly moves at all (−0.026 for the dwell time): the one-second overhead per site dominates, as chapter 7 found. A tool that is to be fast must cut the overhead or measure many features per image, not scan faster.

Key result · what matters most

At the default settings the probe current is by far the most sensitive quantity of the machine: in per cent it changes fifteen to sixteen times as much as the tip radius or the extraction voltage; through the number of electrons it carries that sensitivity into the precision of every measurement. Everything else follows power laws with modest exponents, between −3/4 (the probe against the landing voltage) and +1/2.

8.3Wobbles of a real machine: the tolerance Monte Carlo

No two tips are alike, a lens current drifts, the gun pressure varies, and the wafer surface is never exactly where the focus was set. A tolerance Monte Carlo draws such errors at random, runs the chain for each draw, and looks at the spread of the results. We draw four errors, with spreads that are assumptions of this page, not data of any tool: the tip radius with a relative spread of 3 % (its logarithm normal), the natural logarithm of the gun pressure with a spread of 0.5, the objective excitation with a relative drift ε of standard deviation sI​=10−5, and the wafer height after focusing with 20 nm. They are independent; there are 300 draws with fixed random numbers. The gun is taken without any current control, so a blunter tip gives less current: this shows the raw sensitivity, the worst case. And the aperture stays at the angle that is best for the nominal machine, as a real aperture would, rather than being re-optimised for each draw.

Two of the errors act through the source: the tip radius and the pressure change Br​, ΔE50​ and dv​. The column was set up for the asked current with chapter 2's default tip; with the same acceptance of the column, the current then scales as Br​dv2​ (brightness times source area, which is the angular intensity) and the source image as dv​. The same rule makes the current readout move when the tip or extraction sliders move. Chapter 2 is too slow to run 300 times, so the module runs it on a 5 × 5 grid in tip radius and pressure, spanning three spreads each way, and interpolates (check W4: within 1 % of direct runs; the 2 draws in 300 that fall outside the grid are held at its edge). The other two errors defocus the probe. The lens strength goes as B2/V∗, so an excitation off by the fraction ε acts like a voltage off by −2ε, and since Cc​ is the focus shift per relative change of V∗, the focus moves by

Δz=2Cc​ε,
(8.2)

57.0 nm for ε=10−5; chapter 4's own ray tracer confirms it (check W3). A wafer height error adds to Δz. A beam of half-angle α defocused by Δz is a uniform disc of radius α∣Δz∣, whose FW50 diameter is 2​α∣Δz∣; we add it to the probe in quadrature, a simple rule that is exact for neither shape.

Example 8.2 · the default machine, wobbling

Over the 300 draws the probe varies by 0.10 nm (standard deviation), and the precision is worse than 0.30 nm in 5 % of them. With a specification of 0.25 nm, 80 % of the draws meet it; with 300 draws that share carries a statistical error of about 2 percentage points. Switched on one at a time, the tip radius alone lets 81 % meet it, through the current, and the other three alone let all draws meet it. The lens drift spreads the probe most, by 0.087 nm, but costs little precision; the tip spreads it by 0.038 nm, the wafer height by 0.008 nm; the pressure, at 10−9 Pa an hour after cleaning, does nearly nothing. The result agrees with the sensitivity table: a 3 % spread of the radius times the table's 7.5 spreads the precision by some 20 %, enough to push the upper tail of a 0.20 nm machine past 0.25 nm.

Alignment, which the plan of this project listed, is not among the errors: a beam off the lens axis suffers coma, and we have no source for the coma coefficient of this lens, so we leave it out rather than invent one.

8.4Which settings work: the measurement window

Lithographers draw a process window: the region of focus and exposure in which a pattern prints within specification. A metrology tool has the same kind of map. The left panel of the simulation shows σCD​ over landing voltage (0.5 to 5 kV) and probe current (1 pA to 1 nA), 14 by 14 points, each with the aperture at its best angle. The wine region meets the precision specification, and the darker the grey, the further a point misses it; the dashed line is the dose limit, above which one image would put more than the allowed charge on the wafer (we assume 300 µC cm−2; resists differ widely in how much they tolerate).

Example 8.3 · reading the window

At 0.5 kV the precision goes from 0.58 nm at 1 pA to 0.032 nm at 1 nA; at 5 kV from 1.1 to 0.041 nm. Over the map, more current always helps, though over a factor of a thousand in current the precision improves by less than the 1000​≈32 of pure counting, because the best probe grows with the current. At a given current, low voltage is better: the core and halo of the secondary signal widen and the yield falls as the voltage rises (chapter 6), and the edges soften. The window is bounded above by the dose: at 100 ns per pixel and 1 nm pixels the limit lies at 30 pA, only three times the default current. So at these settings the window is a strip of low voltage between about the default current and the dose limit. The map leaves out further reasons for low voltage, charging of insulators and damage to resist, and the reason for high voltage, seeing buried layers; chapter 7's flat silicon line contains none of them.

Chapter 8 has no Python twin: it adds no physics of its own beyond (8.2) and the current at fixed condensers, and every module it calls is checked against its twin in its own chapter.

What the model leaves out. Everything the earlier chapters leave out, and in addition: the correlations between errors (a blunter tip delivers the same current from a larger area at a lower field, and so with a narrower energy spread), alignment and coma, drift of the gun's own optics, and the coupling of landing voltage and lens (the lens here is computed without a retarding field, chapter 4). The spreads of the tolerance Monte Carlo and the two specifications are assumptions, chosen to show the method; a real tolerance budget starts from measured spreads of a real tool.

Chapter 9The column in one view

The threads of the earlier chapters gathered in one place: why electrons, how a field focuses and why never perfectly, what limits the spot and the measurement, why the cold tip is bright and fragile, what the beam sees, how a width is read, why speed matters, where quantum mechanics enters, and how the numbers were checked. Each paragraph points to the chapter where the argument is worked out.

9.1Why electrons

The case for an electron beam rests on three properties, and the chapters take them in turn. An electron of a few hundred volts has a wavelength of tens of picometres (43.3 pm at 800 V, §3.2), thousands of times shorter than the deep-ultraviolet light of lithography, so diffraction no longer hides a line of twenty nanometres (§0.2). It carries a charge, so electric and magnetic fields can accelerate, steer and focus it (§1.2, §4.3). And it interacts strongly with matter, so it comes back out of a surface carrying information about the top few nanometres (§6.6). X-rays have the short wavelength, but their lenses (zone plates, grazing mirrors) are weak and lose most of the light; ions have the charge, but being heavy they knock atoms out of what they look at. The price of the electron's strong interaction is that it never simply reflects: it wanders inside the wafer, and every image is a blurred and noisy record of that wandering.

9.2How a field focuses, and why never perfectly

A magnetic field does no work, yet a short coil focuses electrons as a glass lens focuses light. The mechanism is a two-step twist. Near the gap the field lines bend, the radial field sets the electron turning about the axis, and the turning motion, crossed with the axial field, pushes it inwards in proportion to its distance from the axis. Busch's theorem makes the first step exact and the paraxial equation r′′=−ηB2r the second (§4.3); the same equation holds for every ray in a frame that turns with the Larmor rate, which is why the image is sharp and rotated. The strength goes as B2/V∗, which is why the same lens serves at every voltage if its current scales as V∗​, and why a lens cannot tell north from south.

What a round magnetic lens can never do is focus all rays alike. Scherzer's theorem says that its spherical and chromatic aberration coefficients are positive for every static, round, charge-free lens that forms a real image (§4.6). Rays at larger angles focus too soon; electrons of different energy focus at different depths. That single fact turns the design of a probe into a compromise, worked out in §5.3.

9.3What limits the spot and the measurement

Four blurs set the size of the probe: diffraction, which shrinks as the beam angle opens; spherical and chromatic aberration, which grow with it; and the image of the source, which shrinks as the angle opens because the same current then needs a smaller source image (§5.1). There is one best angle, and at 800 V on chapter 4's lens it is a balance of diffraction against chromatic aberration (§5.3): 4.11 nm at 8.67 mrad for 10 pA. Higher voltage helps the probe, shorter wavelength and smaller relative energy spread, 0.56 nm at 30 kV with the same lens. The source enters twice: its brightness fixes how much current a given spot can carry, and its energy spread fixes the chromatic blur, which is why a cold field emitter, with its narrow energy distribution, wins at low voltage (§2.7, §5.4).

The measurement adds two limits of its own. The signal does not come from the probe's footprint alone: secondary electrons made by backscattered electrons surface away from the beam, a halo around a sharp core (§6.7). And the signal is counted: electrons arrive one by one, and their shot noise, amplified by the random number of secondaries each frees, sets how precisely an edge can be placed (§7.3). A probe of a few nanometres can still give a width to a few tenths of a nanometre, because many lines and many electrons are averaged; the precision is a statistical quantity, not a picture of the probe.

9.4Why the cold tip is bright and fragile

A cold field emitter draws its electrons by tunnelling through a barrier thinned by a field of several volts per nanometre at a sharp apex (§2.5). The current depends on the field almost exponentially, which makes the source both brilliant and touchy. Brilliant, because electrons leave from a tiny area near the Fermi level with little spread in energy; touchy, because anything that changes the field or the work function changes the current a great deal. A single adsorbed layer of gas raises the work function and dims the patch it covers, which is why the tip lives in a vacuum of order 10−9 Pa and is flashed clean at intervals (§2.10). Chapter 8 measures the same touchiness from the other side: with the optics fixed, the probe current changes fifteen to sixteen times as much, in per cent, as the tip radius or the extraction voltage (§8.2). We infer that this is one reason to run such guns at constant current, with the extraction voltage following the tip.

9.5What the beam sees, and why low voltage

The electrons that make the usual image are secondary electrons, slow electrons freed in the solid, and only those born within a few nanometres of the surface escape (§6.6). That is why the image is a map of the surface, and why edges are bright: a beam that strikes a steep wall crosses the thin escape layer on a slant and frees more secondaries that can get out (§7.1). Backscattered electrons come from deeper and carry more of the material than of the shape.

Landing voltage decides how deep and how wide the beam acts. The range grows faster than the energy, roughly as its five-thirds power in the Kanaya–Okayama law: some twenty nanometres in silicon at 800 V, 9.3 µm at 30 kV (§6.7). At low voltage the energy stays in the top tens of nanometres, near the structure being measured, the halo of the signal is small, and insulating layers can be held near the voltage at which as many electrons leave as arrive, so that they hardly charge (§6.6). At high voltage the beam reaches buried layers, which is useful for seeing through a stack and harmful for a fragile resist. The model of chapter 6 is honest about where it fails: for heavy elements at low voltage it overstates the backscattering, because the Rutherford cross-section is not accurate there.

9.6Reading a width, and how precisely

A width is read from a blurred, noisy profile by a rule, and every rule has a bias and a scatter (§7.4). The bias, a few nanometres for a threshold rule on a dense pattern, is a property of the method and is calibrated against a reference measurement. The scatter is what limits a metrology tool, and it obeys the counting law: it falls as the inverse square root of the number of electrons used (§7.5). Halving it needs four times the electrons, which costs time, and, if they are put on the same pixels, four times the dose. Error propagation predicts the scatter to first order; repeating the noisy measurement in a Monte Carlo checks it, and the two agree within a fifth at ordinary settings and part where the edges are weak.

9.7Speed and statistics

A factory measures not one line but many sites on every wafer, and what it needs is precision per hour. In the model of chapter 7 the time per site is dominated by the overhead of moving, focusing and recognising the pattern, not by the scan (§7.6); a faster scan alone gains little, while measuring many features in one image gains a great deal. Applied Materials' public claim of up to 100 million measurements per hour for its newest tool can only mean many measurements per image; we quote it as a claim and model nothing on it. Chapter 8 adds what a single setting cannot show: which inputs matter most, how much the ordinary wobbles of a machine spread the result, and which settings meet a specification at all (§8.3, §8.4).

9.8Where quantum mechanics enters

Classical mechanics carries most of this project: the trajectories, the lens, the scattering orbits. Quantum mechanics enters at four places, each decisive. The wavelength h/p sets the diffraction limit of the probe (§5.1). Tunnelling through the surface barrier is the field emission of the source, and the Fermi–Dirac distribution of the metal's electrons shapes its energy spread (§2.3, §2.7). The graininess of charge is the shot noise of the measurement (§7.3). And the full quantum treatment of the scattering, the Mott cross-section (exact partial waves with the electron's spin, where the screened Rutherford formula rests on the first Born approximation), is what the simple scattering model of chapter 6 leaves out and pays for with heavy elements.

9.9How the numbers were checked

A simulation is only as good as the evidence that it does what it says. Every number on this page is computed by the project's code and printed from it, never typed. Each module of the browser, except chapter 8's, which only chains the others, has a second, independent version in Python, run on the same inputs; the two agree to the stated tolerance (from 10−15 for closed formulas to about 10−9 where Monte Carlo paths meet library functions). The derivations are checked symbolically with SymPy, and the solvers against exact solutions where one exists: Glaser's lens, the closed-form optimum angles, the free-path and angle laws of the scattering. Published data are shown beside the model with their source, and the gap is stated: the measured backscattering of gold, the secondary yields of Lin and Joy, the stopping powers of NIST, the worked spot of Joy.

Finally, every chapter was read by two independent reviewers who saw only the page, one as a student and expert reader and one who rederived every equation and recomputed every number. They found real errors, and the corrections are recorded in the project's audit. The largest was a misread coefficient: the half-current diameter of the Airy disc had been taken as 0.66 instead of 0.54 times λ/α, which made every probe of chapter 5 a fifth to a quarter too large and invented a disagreement inside a cited paper. Checking against the physics, not against the text, is what found it.
